Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

The booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Log into your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. If you don't have 17,500 miles already, check your transferable points balances:

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

Let's walk through a real scenario that illustrates exactly what this redemption looks like in practice.

The Setup: You've just arrived at London Heathrow on a transatlantic award — perhaps an ANA First Class redemption through the very same Flying Club program. You have a few days in London, and now you need to get to Athens, Greece, where your Mediterranean adventure begins. You check flights: a business class seat on Virgin Atlantic's LHR → ATH route on your target date is priced at $2,200 cash.

The Redemption: You log into virginatlantic.com and find a business class award seat on that same flight: 17,500 Virgin miles + approximately $120 in taxes and fuel surcharges. You have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your ThankYou account from your Citi Premier card. You initiate the transfer — 1:1, instant — and within minutes, your Flying Club account reflects 17,500 miles (with 2,500 to spare for future use). You complete the booking.

The Experience: On the day of travel, you access the Virgin Clubhouse at Heathrow — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world. The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Do this: Search 331 days out for peak season Virgin's booking window opens exactly 331 days before departure. For summer travel to Athens, Rome, or other peak European destinations, business class award inventory gets claimed early. Set a phone reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date. Log in that morning. The seats that seem impossible to find in the 60-day window are often available the moment the calendar rolls over.

Do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. If you send 17,500 Chase points over and then discover the seat isn't actually available (or you misread the cabin class), those miles are stuck in Flying Club. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. They don't destroy the CPP math, but they're a genuine cash cost you need to plan around.

Do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

The ideal candidate is someone who's already planning a trip that routes through London Heathrow — perhaps on a transatlantic award — and needs an elegant, high-value way to reach their final European destination. Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. At 17,500 miles per person, a couple needs 35,000 Virgin miles, which is completely achievable with a single transfer from a combined Chase or Amex balance.

Families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. Multiplying 17,500 miles per person across four or more travelers creates a significant points requirement, and availability for multiple seats on the same flight is far from guaranteed. The fuel surcharges also multiply with passenger count. Families are better served by other redemption strategies.

This is NOT for beginners. The overall score of 2.7/5 and beginner-friendliness rating of 1/5 signal real complexity. If you're just starting your travel rewards journey, build your foundation with simpler redemptions first. But if you've got a year of points accumulation behind you and you're ready to think architecturally about trip planning, this sweet spot can be a revelatory experience.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally shows availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Log into VirginAtlantic.com and search for reward flights in Upper Class (business) on your desired European route. Look for VS-coded flights only. Ignore partner-operated results, which will price differently.

Midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

The Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.

#8539. Canada Coast to Coast Paddlers Begin Final Stretch

Canadian paddlers Will Vyse and Nolan Aziz — reduced to a twosome after Georges Kirijian left the expedition with an injury — are entering the final stretch of their mammoth 8,000km expedition from Tadoussac, Quebec, to Vancouver, British Columbia, on the Pacific Ocean.

After 184 days, including 34 days in Alberta, they crossed into British Columbia on October 10. This marks the final province of their trip. They have recently been paddling up the Peace River, which they describe as “long and arduous.”  The canoeists have covered well over 6,000km, and both they and their gear look suitably disheveled:

Once they finish with the Peace River, they have a meaty 17km portage to Williston Lake, the largest lake in British Columbia, before taking the southern branch of the Crooked River. After crossing the Continental Divide and completing the Giscome Portage between Summit Lake and the Fraser River, they will take the Fraser through Prince George and down to Vancouver.

Vyse and Aziz originally planned to end their trip in the town of Prince Rupert, but have since altered their route to finish at Vancouver’s Wreck Beach.

“Our reroute maintains a total expedition distance of over 8,000km, and upon completion will still be the longest ever recorded single-season canoe trip,” Vyse and Aziz wrote on social media.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8538. Google’s Collapse Gives Hope for the Middle Class and Our Kids

I’ve been a Google shareholder since 2010 and I'm thankful. But yesterday’s earnings, and the 12% collapse that followed, left me thoroughly disappointed.

Search is under siege. Gemini isn’t leading the AI race. And Google is spending like a drunken sailor to catch up.

Spending $200 billion in CAPEX is more than the GDP of most countries. And free cash flow just went negative $9 billion for the quarter.

What does $200 billion buy you? Third or fourth place in the AI race, depending on who you ask. Behind Anthropic. Behind OpenAI. Maybe neck and neck with whoever else is closing fast.

That’s pathetic. And as a shareholder, it’s demoralizing. Not even Berkshire Hathaway investing $10 billion at $350/share can save us.

Google researchers wrote the 2017 paper that introduced the transformer, the “T” in ChatGPT. Google owns DeepMind. It designs its own TPU chips. It has Search, YouTube, Android, Gmail, and roughly 3 billion Chrome users. It understood large language models years before most of us knew what it was.

And yet most developers aren’t coding with Gemini. They’re using Claude Code, Codex, or something else.

In the most transformational technology since the internet went mainstream, Google had a ten-mile head start, outspent nearly everyone, and still got lapped.

Meanwhile, executives collected enormous pay packages. Nice work, which most of us can't get.

Everybody in the Bay Area knows Google is one of the best places to “rest and vest.” HBO’s Silicon Valley spoofed it with Big Head, who got promoted at Hooli into a big title, a rooftop office, and zero responsibilities.

Who doesn’t want to get paid a lot to work less? Of course there are plenty of hard-working people at Google.

But resting and vesting only feels good when the stock keeps going up. When the stock stalls, you’re just resting and asking whether this is all there is to life.

I’ve seen this movie before. I left Credit Suisse in 2012 partly because technology was squeezing the business. Algorithmic trading was compressing commissions toward zero, which is why trading is basically free today.

Our Asian equities group was competitive. But the firm overall was lagging Goldman, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and UBS. Staying at a firm falling behind, in an industry being hollowed out, felt like polishing brass on a sinking ship.

So I left to build my own thing. I made a fraction of my old income for years. But watching something I built actually grow was more thrilling than any bonus check.

Momentum is energizing. Decline is a slow poison, even when the paycheck clears.

Part of the reason I invested in Google was its dominance. Two Stanford PhD students, who fittingly never finished their PhDs, hired an army of brilliant nerds from Stanford, MIT, and the Indian Institute of Technology.

They commanded over 90% search market share. They piled up over $100 billion in cash. Then they used monopoly profits to enter new businesses and crush the competition.

In other words, Google became the trust fund kid. Let’s call him Chip.

Chip was born on third base. Parent's money, the search monopoly, pays for everything. Grandpa’s name is on the library, which is the transformer paper and DeepMind. Family friends can make one phone call and open any door, which is Android, Chrome, and the default search deal with Apple.

Chip still posts on Instagram about his “grind” while sipping a $28 smoothie.

Everybody else in the AI race is the middle-class or poor kid. There is no way Chip should lose his incredible head start, unless he really messes up.

OK, maybe I’m being a little extreme. OpenAI has Microsoft’s money. Anthropic has Amazon’s money. Their founders went to Princeton, Stanford, and other elite schools. Nobody here is eating ramen.

But wealth is relative. If everybody is a millionaire, nobody is rich. Next to Google, everybody is middle class.

Google started the AI race with billions of users, a cash machine, and its own chips. Everyone else started with zero users and had to beg investors for money just to rent compute. Every dollar they raised came with a pitch deck and a deadline.

The middle-class kid has to justify every dollar. The trust fund kid just asks Dad for $200 billion.

And here’s the most trust fund kid thing of all. Google is an investor in Anthropic. Chip is literally paying tuition for the kid who’s beating him.

As a capitalist, you usually don’t bet against Chip when he’s smart and connected. You invest in him. I’ve watched the kid with every advantage win since 2004, when Google went public.

But every so often, Chip gets comfortable. He takes a third gap year. He hires expensive consultants to tell him what he should already know. Shiny object syndrome takes hold, and financial resources and attention get diverted to solving core problems.

Meanwhile, the middle-class kid has no safety net. If he doesn’t ship, he doesn’t eat.

Dario Amodei is a good example. He grew up middle class in San Francisco. His dad was a leather craftsman. His mom managed library projects. He went to Lowell, a public high school, studied hard, and actually finished his PhD.

In 2021, he co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela and a group of colleagues. Five years later, Claude is what developers reach for, and Anthropic is one of the most valuable private companies on earth.

It’s Google versus the world. And the world is the rest of us.

The trust fund kid has every advantage except one. He doesn’t need to win.

The middle-class kid has only one advantage. He must win or be relegated to the permanent underclass.

Hunger is the great equalizer. And unlike a trust fund, it can’t be inherited.

There’s another reason I’m not shedding too many tears for Chip, even though my portfolio needs to go to the ER. For years, he’s been taking other people’s lunch money.

Google built its empire by sending traffic to websites like mine. That was the deal. Bloggers, journalists, and small publishers created the content. Google organized it, sold ads around it, and sent readers our way. Everybody ate.

First came featured snippets, which lifted our answers onto the results page so readers didn’t need to click. Then Google stuffed its own products at the top: shopping results, travel results, maps, “People also ask” boxes, and more ads. The organic results, the content people actually searched for, got pushed so far down you needed a scuba tank to find them.

Then came AI Overviews. Now Google reads our work, summarizes it, and serves it as its own answer at the top of the page. The attribution, if there is any, is a tiny link most people never click.

Imagine writing from firsthand experience since 2009, only to watch a multi-trillion-dollar company repackage your insights and keep the reader. That’s not a search engine. That’s a very polite pickpocket.

And yes, I know the AI companies trained on publishers’ work too without attribution or payment. You have to steal people’s work to get rich sometimes. Nobody in this race has clean hands. But Google was supposed to be the partner. It sent us traffic for two decades before deciding it would rather keep it. So now it stomps on us too.

I don’t want to oversell the hope. Since graduating college in 1999, I’ve watched the rich get far richer than everybody else.

The first reason is math. The rich have more capital, so a bull market hands them bigger absolute dollar gains. The longer compounding runs, the bigger the pile gets.

I saw it at Goldman in NYC, at Credit Suisse in SF, and every year since I left in 2012. Some friends from my tennis club who were mere millionaires 15 years ago are now multi-billionaires.

The second reason is proximity. Rich people mostly hang out with other rich people. And proximity creates opportunity.

Once you’re an LP, you might get invited to co-invest in a hot private AI company the fund has high conviction in. That’s how the gap widens, one quiet invitation at a time. Be nice and helpful to as many people as possible.

Everybody rolls their eyes at networking. I hated it too. It’s likely the main reason I never made Managing Director. I couldn’t fake enough agreeableness with the powers that be.

The lesson to pass to our kids: you don’t have to be fake. But you do have to show up and always play nice with others if you want to get ahead

The beauty of FIRE is freedom. The problem with being a FIRE parent is that your network withers once you leave the workforce.

The people who could introduce you to clients, write a preschool recommendation letter, or refer you for a better job slowly disappear. And if you’re truly FIRE, you stop caring about getting ahead. Otherwise you’d still be trading time for money.

Then you have kids. And suddenly, money and status matter again in a hurry.

That’s why Google’s stumble actually provides hope, despite the paper loss.

If a company with $100 billion in cash, 3 billion users, the transformer itself, and a $200 billion annual budget can fumble its lead, then advantages aren’t destiny. They’re a head start. And head starts can be squandered.

Which means a hungry kid with no connections still has a real shot. So does the poorest minority kid in America.

My children won’t inherit a monopoly. But they can inherit a work ethic, some hunger, and the knowledge that Chip can be beaten.

Look, you’ve had a great run. Thank you for your hard work all these years. Google’s strategic drift isn’t your fault. That’s on the C-suite.

But as a shareholder, I have two requests.

This is wartime, not peacetime. Mass layoffs are likely coming, and the people who survive them tend to be the ones who are visibly in the building.

It’s been fun playing pickleball with many of you at 11:30 a.m. on a Tuesday. I’ll miss the competition. But that has to stop now.

The stock could be dead money for a year or two while the supertanker turns. If you’re only staying for the next vest, you’re not resting. You’re rotting.

Golden handcuffs are still handcuffs. And gold is heavy.

Go be the middle-class kid again in your own career. Join or start something where you have to win. That’s what Jeff Dean and colleagues did with the launch of Discovery Loop.

What doesn’t work is the middle path: staying, coasting, and feeling empty. That’s the worst of both worlds for you and for us shareholders. If you decide to leave, please try to negotiate a severance package. You have nothing to lose.

Google has the resources to recover. Trust fund kids usually get a second or third chance. The only question is whether Chip still wants it badly enough. It’s hard when you’re already so rich.

Readers, do you think Google can regain its AI lead, or has the trust fund kid permanently lost his edge? Is spending $200 billion a year a sign of strength or desperation? If you work at a big tech company, are you resting and vesting, or quietly planning your exit? And as a parent, how are you teaching your kids to compete without a trust fund or a powerful network?

Google now summarizes bloggers' work at the top of the page and keeps the reader. So the best way to get my firsthand takes on money, investing, AI, and raising kids is straight from the source.

100% disagree! As someone working inside Google Cloud after spending 6 years at AWS, I see a very different reality than the doomsday narrative around Google’s future.

Second, the broader market seems to miss where modern AI actually runs. People talk about third-party models like Claude disrupting Search, but we need to remember where Anthropics cores are physically hosted: Google Cloud. For every consumer query dollar that might shift away from legacy search, a substantial portion gets pushed right back into GCP enterprise spend.

Third, look at the underlying economics. GCP’s 103% YoY acceleration in AI compute isn’t just vanity growth, the margins on AI infrastructure are very favorable. More importantly, these cores creates a massive gravitational drag: when enterprises come for our TPUs and GPUs, they bring their standard compute, high-throughput storage, databases (Spanner, AlloyDB), and analytics (BigQuery) with them. That is exceptionally sticky, high-margin revenue.

Alphabet trading near a 14 P/E (historically cheap) suggests the market is pricing in terminal search decay while ignoring the enterprise cloud engine right in front of them. The sentiment gap is wide, which is exactly why I continue to invest.

#8537. Giant Crabs Complicate New Amelia Earhart Search

Researchers hunting for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s plane have followed new clues to a remote Pacific atoll, inhabited by giant coconut crabs so large and active at night that the team sleeps aboard its ship for safety.

In 1932, the American aviation pioneer became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. Five years later, she and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared while attempting to circumnavigate the globe. After leaving Papua New Guinea on July 2, they failed to reach Howland Island, their planned refueling stop. The official account is that navigation and communication problems caused their Lockheed Electra to run out of fuel and crash into the ocean. The disappearance has produced decades of speculation about what happened.

Amelia Earhart beside her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. 1937. Photo: National Portrait Gallery

One long-standing hypothesis, advanced mainly by the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, is that the pair reached Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), about 350 nautical miles southeast of Howland, landed on the reef, and later died as castaways.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University arrived at the uninhabited atoll — part of Kiribati — this week after a 1,500km voyage on their vessel, according to the BBC and Purdue University updates. They are investigating the Taraia Object, an elongated shape in a lagoon first identified in satellite imagery in 2020 and visible in aerial photos dating to 1938.

Some researchers view it as a possible remnant of Earhart’s plane. Others consider it more likely a fallen tree or other debris. This marks the first authorized visit to the island in seven years, and the first to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15 years.

The uninhabited Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean. Photo: Wikipedia

The work, which should take about five days, includes clearing vegetation, scanning for metal, and using dredging equipment to examine the object, which lies only about three meters from shore in as little as 1.5m of water, depending on the tides. Conditions have already limited boat access on some days, though organizers expect an update on the object’s identity within about 48 hours, according to Purdue.

The coconut crab has the strongest pinch of any crustacean. Photo: Reinhard Dirscherl via treehugger.com

The island’s coconut crabs, also called robber crabs, are the world’s largest land-dwelling invertebrates, with a leg span of up to one meter and a body weight of more than four kilos. They can lift objects weighing about 28kg, crack open coconuts, climb trees, and emerge at night to capture live prey such as rats and seabirds, as well as carrion. Expedition communications stated that the crabs’ size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical, so the crew returns to the ship each night.

The same animals appear in theories about what might have happened if Earhart died on Nikumaroro. In 1940, British colonists recovered 13 bones near the remains of a fire. The bones were later lost, though some re-analyses of the recorded measurements have suggested consistency with a woman of Earhart’s stature.

The Taraia Object on a satellite image. Photo: Rick Pettigrew/Archaeological Legacy Institute

In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery placed pig carcasses on a similar island and found that coconut crabs (along with smaller hermit crabs) stripped most of the flesh and dragged bones to burrows in less than two weeks. The crabs are not known to hunt humans aggressively. The primary risk is a powerful defensive pinch from their claws if they are handled or startled.

The survey of the Taraia Object began on Wednesday. The crew established a base camp, cleared overgrown paths, and prepared for their fieldwork.

Previous searches, including one by well-known explorer Robert Ballard, who first located the Titanic, have not produced any aircraft wreckage, and many experts continue to regard an ocean crash near Howland as the most likely outcome. The current team reports encountering some crabs during initial setup but described them as posing no threat to operations at that stage.

The Taraia Object’s survey has begun. Photo: Purdue.edu

#8536. Image of Elephant Carrying Dead Calf Wins Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

Federico Veronesi was following a family of elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he came upon a strange and tragic sight. A female elephant was carrying the stiff body of a deceased calf. The Italian wildlife photographer’s shocking image has become the Grand Title Winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Earlier, we reviewed the runner-up entries for this year, released back in September. One of those entries included Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen’s photo of an orca carrying a deceased calf, which it repeatedly lifted up out of the water. These striking images of animals mourning speak to the contest’s mission. Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum, says it strives to “demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently.”

Other category winners explore the relationship between the wild and urban worlds, document natural beauty, and capture more playful wildlife moments.

Winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category, Alex Visbal’s image shows how artificially dividing a Utah wetland has cut part of it off from freshwater, resulting in pink-producing, high-salinity microbes. Photo: Alex Visbal/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

While images like Visbal and Veronesi’s capture large scenes and massive animals, other winners focus on tiny, hidden natural worlds. Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas of Germany won the Rising Star Portfolio Award for his series exploring the smallest and least noticed animals.

As not all of our readers are as fond of arachnids as I am, we feature Tinker-Tsavalas’ whimsical image of a teensy springtail exploring moss, rather than his portraits of ground crab spiders or harvestmen. Photo: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Below even the insect level are the works of macro photographer Kutub Uddin. He won the Portfolio Award for his series of surreal slime mold landscapes. Like Tinker-Tsavalas, Uddin uses focus stacking to achieve incredible fine detail.

This fruiting slime mold looks like some sort of whimsical, slightly grotesque bonsai. Photo: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Several winners focused on wildlife in non-wild settings. Loren Elliott won the Photojournalist Story Award for his series following the coyotes of San Francisco. There are around 100 coyotes living in and around San Francisco, and their relationship with human residents is close, but fraught.

There were several excellent shots in this series, but I would be failing you if I didn’t highlight this one. These two coyote pups live in a den on a golf course, leaving them plenty of golf balls to play with. Photo: Loren Elliott/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Across the world in Bangkok, common water monitors have also become city dwellers. Seth Forestson won in the Urban Wildlife category for his image of a lizard triumphantly bearing a fish through a public park. In the background, the city skyline rises in dramatic contrast.

Photo: Seth Forestson/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Meanwhile, the Plants and Fungi category winner comes from the weird world of mushrooms. On Mount Olympus, Agorastos Papatsanis used ultraviolet light to reveal the luminescence of Mycena renati. Commonly known as beautiful bonnet, the stems of these mushrooms glow a neon yellow.

Photo: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

The Young Grand Title Winner, who entered in the 11-14 year-old category, is Oscar Whitfield. In Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park, Whitfield captured the efforts of a dung beetle.

Ancient Egyptian cosmology drew parallels between the scarab beetle, pushing a ball of dung, and Khepri, the scarab-headed deity, pushing the sun across the sky. The dung beetle also plays a vital role environmentally. The way they process and bury dung reduces methane production and helps speed decomposition. Photo: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

You can view the full gallery on the Natural History Museum website. Tickets to the full exhibition in London, England are available here.

The full view of Federico Veronesi’s contest-winning image. Photo: Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8535. Summits Begin on Ama Dablam, Late Fall's Most Popular Peak

With the failure of commercial climbs on Manaslu and Dhaulagiri this fall, all eyes now turn to the most popular commercial peak in the second half of autumn — 6,812m Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team already opened the route to the summit last Tuesday.

Unlike those two 8,000m peaks, where bad conditions prompted outfitters to abort the season prematurely, the seven rope fixers on Ama Dablam experienced light winds, sunshine, and good snow, which allowed them to fix 800m of rope in just five hours. Siddhi Bahadur Tamang, Lal Kumar Tamang, Dawa Paljor Sherpa, Lakpa Sangay Sherpa, Pasang Tenji Sherpa, and Namgel Dorje Tamang stood on top of Ama Dablam on October 13 shortly before noon:

Since then, workers have been hurrying to set up and stock three higher camps, while many climbers flock to Base Camp or acclimatize on nearby peaks before their summit push.

According to the October 13 update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism, 178 permits for foreign climbers have been issued for Ama Dablam. That will increase greatly over the coming weeks, since the high season continues until the end of November. In recent years, improved logistics and increased popularity have led to many more summits. Success rates are also far better than just a few years ago.

Last fall, according to the Himalayan Database (HDB), 273 foreigners attempted to climb — and all succeeded! They were supported by 399 Sherpas, including guides, high-altitude porters, and their helpers. The final summit numbers included the 273 foreigners plus 227 locals, totaling 500 summits, with a 100% summit rate. Two clients died: a Brazilian climber hit by falling ice on his way down, and a South Korean man who suffered cardiac arrest.

By comparison, in 2015, 76 foreigners and 47 locals summited — nearly five times fewer — and the summit rate was 71%. Certain things have not changed: Back then, the normal route was also fixed, and teams had Sherpa support. It’s the scale and the tactics that are different.

Ama Dablam Base Camp. Photo: Dominic Asselin

If Everest is to Himalayan climbing history what Mont Blanc was to the Alps, Ama Dablam is the Nepalese equivalent of the Matterhorn: a favorite of both climbers and outfitters, for different reasons.

Climbers appreciate its beauty — it’s usually considered one of the most aesthetic peaks in the world, despite its commercialization, with ropes, abundant Sherpa support, and helicopter transfers. Moreover, the views of Everest, Lhotse, and the surrounding peaks from its flat, snowy summit are breathtaking:

Its relatively low altitude means shorter acclimatization. Climbers usually do a trekking peak and/or hypoxic training at home as preparation. An Ama Dablam climb rarely requires supplemental oxygen — although it is available if needed.

Its convenient location in the Khumbu Valley on the way to Everest is a great asset, thanks to its many year-round accommodations, good infrastructure, an easy peak to acclimatize for, and a straightforward approach trek.

A crowded camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Lakpa Sherpa/8K Expeditions

For outfitters, Ama Dablam is a natural moneymaker. Its wide Base Camp on a dry, flat plain allows a large number of tents, a helipad, and the constant flow of supplies from the Khumbu’s main trail nearby. Yet the key to accommodating many climbers lies in fast expeditions. Once acclimatized, climbers can summit Ama Dablam and return down in three or four days — even less for the frequent speed climbers. That allows companies to reuse the tents and equipment many times through the season. Camp staff and guides are constantly working, with little downtime.

As for the climb itself, double ropes allow climbers to ascend and descend at the same time, maintaining a steady flow of people every day while the weather holds. Last year, there were 10 to 30 summits a day between October 12 and October 27, and nearly every day in November.

File image of climbers on Ama Dablam, progressing on fixed ropes. Photo: Explore-Share

Even during winter, which in Nepal officially starts on December 1, it is common for some teams to attempt Ama Dablam, especially before the end of the year. Expert winter climbers such as Simone Moro often mention the cold but stable and sunny days in Nepal in December. In recent winter attempts on Manaslu, Moro has acclimatized on Ama Dablam.

Nima Rinji, Simone Moro, and Oswald Pereira acclimatized on Ama Dablam in December 2024 before attempting Manaslu in winter. Photo: Manish Maharjan

Last year, the HDB only registered a three-member expedition that summited the mountain in winter. However, during the 2024-25 cold season, 12 foreign climbers and six Sherpas summited that December.

Ama Dablam was first climbed in March 1961 by Mike Gill and Wally Romanes of New Zealand, Mike Ward of the UK, and Barry Bishop of the U.S. via the Southwest Ridge.

Some local operators keep a functioning Base Camp and maintained route on Ama Dablam throughout December. Photo: Seven Summit Treks

With all this latter-day success and improved logistics, the biggest risk may be underestimating Ama Dablam. A high number of rescues have occurred in the last few years. Helicopters can perform long-line airlifts from Camp 3, but such options are not available in bad weather. The prospect of a rescue helicopter on standby in case of trouble, especially on the way down, may produce a false sense of security for those who find themselves at their limits but still decide to continue to the summit.

While the death rates on Ama Dablam are relatively low, it is not a peak to be trifled with, as the many cases of frostbite, AMS, and injuries from falling rock and ice attest.

A helicopter performs a rescue at Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Nga Tenji Sherpa

#8534. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:30 pm

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

This is an interesting debate – the people with the most knowledge of AI’s technical details do indeed worry about problems with the intelligence itself, if it comes out not aligned with our own interests.

Early in my career as a self-employed contractor, I would call up my buddy regularly to worry aloud how would I ever have enough work to feed my growing family.

This fear was valid. If I wanted them to eat, I had to buy food. If I wanted to buy food I needed money. To get money I needed paid work. To get paid work I had to sell jobs.

My buddy eventually reminded me that in between calling him up to worry aloud about not having enough work, I would also call him up regularly to beg him to help me with all the work I suddenly had lined up and now I wasn’t sure how I would get it all done!

Until he put it to me that way, I was too caught up in the moment to realize what I had been doing.

So, which is it? Are we afraid of not having enough? Or are we afraid of having too much?

Let’s not be afraid of either one. Either way, we are adaptable, capable and full of badassity!

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 9:09 am

Yeah, it’s not perfect, but I have actually noticed the opposite effect – really good answers to my technical carpentry questions about electrical, plumbing, and even structural work. Apparently it partly depends on what model you’re using.

If you just type a question into Google or whatever, the AI-boosted search mode will give you slightly better answers than the old google would have given. But if you’re using Claude/Gemini/ChatGPT pro and phrase your question specifically, like “is this ground wire connection in my subpanel consistent with the 2024 IRC building code”, and send it a picture of your work, it will do some real building inspector wizardry for you (which I have gone into the code to verify and been shocked at the accuracy). It has already helped me countless times in fixing houses, bikes, cars, whatever.

One other place where it blew my mind – in a recent renovation, I wanted to know if a support beam I found in a ceiling was up to code given the span and the amount of floor it was holding up. It broke down the entire calculation based on floor area, l/360 deflection and all of that and confirmed a bunch of stuff that would have taken me MUCH longer to figure out (or required an expensive email exchange with a structural engineer). I did go in and spot check its numbers, but it got them right. The real value was in finding exactly the right formula for the situation, almost instantly.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:24 pm

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

More fun details on this, one of my favorite subjects, here! https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2022/01/11/inflation-should-we-be-worried/

For example, not only can it transcribe a meeting but it can then analyze the motivations and emotions of each participant at each point in the meeting, or identify whether there were any contradictions to what the CEO said to you versus what was in the 50-page employment contract you also fed to that AI. One time I pressed a bit further with questions and we got into things like a descent into autocratic rule, which would lead to a Venezuela-type wipeout of our economy and loss of all our property, and of course there’s the common refrain of “I think I’ll just move to Canada” that many of my fellow Americans tend to say every time the elections go a certain way.

Call me a blind optimist, but I think the USA is going to remain a wealthy and productive economy which respects personal property rights, regardless of which party is in office. Not everything will be perfect, but life will be a lot better the less you read the daily news.
