#8436. Appalachian Trail Gear: What Worked, What Didn’t, and What I Changed (Part 1)

I found that, just like in the real world, things break, wear out, and sometimes need to be replaced. Just as you budget for an unexpected car repair, you need to plan for gear replacements on the trail. Your shoes aren’t going to last the entire hike (mine lasted about 500 miles!), and sometimes things break when you least expect them.

Take my sleeping pad, for example. It unexpectedly started losing air, and thankfully, my hiking buddy let me borrow his “trail couch,” a foam sleeping pad, until I made it to Daleville, Virginia. Then there are the upgrades you might choose to make along the way. Maybe you realize you can get by with a smaller, lighter tent and decide it’s worth the investment to shed some weight from your pack.

The point is, preparing for a thru-hike isn’t just about buying all your gear before you start. It’s also about budgeting for the things that will wear out, break, or simply need an upgrade along the way. Just like maintaining a car or keeping up with home repairs, taking care of your gear is part of the journey.

I started and ended with a Base Weight of about 13.5 lbs without food, fuel, or water.

So, let’s look at the gear I started with, what held up, what I replaced along the way, and what I carried to the finish line.

I won’t go into a deep dive on my entire gear list, but if you’re curious about the specifics, you can check out my full gear list that I started with on my profile here and what I finished with on LighterPack here.

What I Started With: Big Agnes Tiger Wall UL2

What I Finished With: Hyperlite Mountain Gear Crosspeak 1

I had plenty of experience with the gear I started with, and honestly, it worked! I loved pretty much everything I owned, so I didn’t see a reason to replace perfectly good gear just to upgrade to the latest and trendiest options. That said, I did budget for a new tent.

Originally, I planned to start with the Zpacks Duplex, a tent my fiancé and I use on our backpacking trips. The only catch? He’s usually the one who sets it up for us. Since this was going to be a solo adventure, I needed to be confident setting up my own shelter. It was the middle of winter in Vermont before my hike, and after a few unsuccessful attempts at practicing on my own in the snow, I just wasn’t feeling confident enough to bring it along.

Instead, I decided to start with my Big Agnes Tiger Wall UL2. At 2.5 pounds, it’s a freestanding tent that’s practically dummy-proof, offers plenty of space, and, most importantly, was something I had tons of experience setting up on my own.

First time pitching my new Crosspeak 1 tent.

I love freestanding tents, but I had my eye on a Dyneema version. The one I wanted wasn’t scheduled to hit the market until April, so my plan was to use the Tiger Wall until it launched. Easy enough, right? Well, then a material issue delayed the release.

Meanwhile, Hyperlite Mountain Gear launched its CrossPeak 1 at Trail Days, and they were offering a deal on it. I didn’t hesitate for a second. I may have downsized on space, but this tent checked a lot of boxes for me and was worth the upgrade.

What I Started With: Gossamer Gear Gorilla 50L

What I Finished With: Gossamer Gear Mariposa 60L

I’ve been a huge fan of Gossamer Gear packs ever since hiking the Wonderland Trail in 2023. In 2024, I invested in the Gorilla 50L for my Tahoe Rim Trail thru-hike, and it turned out to be the perfect pack for me and my needs. So naturally, I figured I’d take it along for the Appalachian Trail. No regrets… at least at first!

The first two months on the AT were pretty dry, and I sometimes found myself carrying up to 4L of water to ‘dry camps’. Resupply options were also more spread out than I expected, which meant carrying five to six days of food at a time. The Gorilla is designed to comfortably carry around 25 pounds, with a recommended maximum of 30 pounds, and I found myself pushing those limits pretty regularly.

My beloved Gorilla started ripping on both sides of the bottom corners.

Eventually, my lower back started chafing from the pack rubbing against it, and the side seams began to split. I was so sad because I genuinely loved this pack! The removable back foam pad doubles as both a frame and a sit pad, which is such a great feature. The side pockets are positioned at just the right height, making it SUPER easy to grab my water bottle and slide it back in without stopping or asking someone for help. And the large exterior mesh pocket? Another favorite.

Rather than give up on Gossamer Gear altogether, I decided to stick with the brand and upgrade to its larger pack, the Mariposa 60L. With a maximum recommended load of around 35 pounds, it seemed like the perfect solution for my heavier carries. I never ended up maxing it out, and it gave me the extra capacity I needed.

Eventually, I also got better at dialing in my resupplies, and my water carries dropped back down to around 2L. But even with the lighter loads, I struggled with the Mariposa for a long time. I’m not entirely sure why, but it felt and sat so differently from my Gorilla. I even had the Gossamer Gear team fit me at Trail Days, yet I still felt like the pack I’d purchased was too small for me.

Over time, it seemed to get more comfortable. Or maybe I just got used to the pain and discomfort. Honestly, I’m still torn about whether the Mariposa will be the pack I reach for on my next thru-hike or if I’ll be looking elsewhere. I loved my Gorilla, but my experience with the Mariposa left me with some mixed feelings about what pack comes next.

Navigating the large boulders on the way up Mama K, featuring my Mariposa.

What I Started With: Enlightened Equipment Enigma 20-degree down

What I Finished With: Enlightened Equipment Revelation APEX 40-degree synthetic

I started the trail March 9th with a 20-degree down quilt, but by the time I reached Pearisburg, Virginia, I was ready to make the switch to my 40-degree synthetic quilt.

For me, the 20-degree quilt just wasn’t the right fit for the entire trail. I tend to run hot, and even early on, I found myself getting too warm at night. I was more than happy to swap it out for the lighter, cooler 40-degree option when I had the chance.

Of course, there were still colder nights ahead, especially once I reached the White Mountains in New Hampshire. When temperatures dropped, I made do with what I had, occasionally pulling my rain pants over my wool baselayer tights for a little extra warmth.

Looking back, I’m glad I made the switch. I didn’t need a 20-degree quilt for the entire trail, and having the option to adjust my sleep system as the seasons and temperatures changed worked out really well for me.

What I used: Therm-a-rest NeoAir Xlite Regular Wide

Good sleep is SO important on the trail. When you’re hiking all day, having a comfortable place to rest and recover at night makes a huge difference. I’ve had this sleeping pad for a few years now, and I absolutely love it.

I originally had the regular size but found it too narrow, especially as a woman and a side sleeper. So, I invested in the Regular Wide, and it’s been perfect for me. This version also has an improved inflation valve, and I find it a bit quieter than the original model and some of the other sleeping pads on the market.

Remember what I mentioned earlier about budgeting for gear repairs and replacements? Well, here’s a perfect example.

5-mile trail NERO, it dumped rain, and many of us called it a day and squeezed into a shelter by 2 pm.

I’m guessing that on my last night before reaching Pearisburg, Virginia, I managed to puncture my sleeping pad. It was pouring rain, and honestly, I was just happy to find a spot, get my tent up, and crawl into something dry. Somewhere in that process, I must have pitched my tent over a stick or something sharp.

I didn’t notice anything was wrong until my first night back on the trail after taking a zero in Pearisburg. My pad was noticeably deflated. I figured it was probably just the temperature change, so I blew it back up and went to sleep. Except I found myself doing that two more times before morning.

I tried all the usual tricks to find the leak. I inflated the pad, pushed down on it, listened for escaping air, and ran my hands all over the surface, hoping to feel even the tiniest bit of air escaping. I even attempted the water-and-soap trick, but no luck. I just couldn’t find the hole.

Thankfully, my trail buddy Viking came to the rescue and lent me his foam sleeping pad until we reached Daleville, Virginia. I was incredibly grateful, but I’m not going to lie, those few nights sleeping on what felt like the bare ground were rough!

When it came time to replace it, there wasn’t much debating what to buy. I loved this sleeping pad enough to purchase the exact same one. Sometimes you find gear that just works for you, and there’s no reason to mess with a good thing.

These trekking poles were a gift from my fiancé, and one of the things I loved most about them was how incredibly lightweight they are. They’re among the lightest options out there, weighing 4.9oz per pole. I was a little surprised that I didn’t see more of them on the trail. Maybe it’s the nearly $200 price tag, or perhaps people are hesitant about investing in carbon fiber poles because of the possibility of them breaking.

I saw plenty of bent poles and broken tips along the way, but guess what? My LT5s survived all 2,200 miles without a single bent shaft or even needing a replacement tip!

Well, almost all 2,200 miles. One of my poles did decide to go on its own solo adventure by leaping into the Delaware River. I had set the pair down while stopping to take a photo at the Pennsylvania–New Jersey state line, and apparently, one decided it had somewhere else to be. I’ll give Gossamer Gear this: these poles do float! Unfortunately, I couldn’t get the attention of any of the paddlers below to help rescue it.

The one pole that decided to stay with me to Katahdin. The other went on its own solo adventure into the Delaware.

I reached out to Gossamer Gear, and they were incredibly kind and sent me a replacement. So, while I technically lost one pole to the Delaware, I was able to finish with a full set.

My one complaint with these poles is the twist-lock adjustment mechanism. It tends to get stuck, and there were plenty of times I had to wrestle with it to get the poles adjusted. Sometimes I’d even hand them over to Jerzy to manhandle them for me!

Despite that one frustration, I was really happy with these poles. They’re lightweight, held up remarkably well over the entire trail, and I’d happily recommend them to someone looking to save weight on their setup.

What I Finished With: Altra Olympus 275 Matryx

I’ve been an Altra fan since 2018. I’ve tried Hoka, I’ve tried Topo, and nothing has quite compared to the zero-drop platform and roomy toe box that Altra offers.

I started the AT with the Olympus 6. I’ll admit, I wasn’t completely sold on this version when I first tried it the summer before my thru-hike. The fit felt a little different from previous versions, and I wasn’t a fan of that odd little heel pillow. But overall, the shoe worked well for me, and I got about 500 miles out of that first pair.

New on the right vs. old pair on the left that I had since Marion, VA, to 501 Shelter in PA.

One of my favorite things about the Olympus is the extra cushioning. When you’re putting in miles day after day, that added cushion makes a big difference. I did experience some heel blisters, particularly along the sides of my heels. Over time, those eventually turned into pretty impressive calluses. As the shoes approached the end of their life, the blisters and foot fatigue became my signal that it was time for a new pair.

That decision came when I stopped at Marion Outdoors to replace my shoes. That’s where I was introduced to the Olympus 275 Matryx. It offered the familiar fit and features I loved, but instead of the heel pillow, it had a built-in gaiter guard.

I still preferred wearing my separate gaiters with these shoes. Although the built-in gaiter guard meant there weren’t traditional gaiter attachment points, I found a workaround. I simply hooked the front of my gaiters onto my shoelaces. The outfitter initially gave me some adhesive Velcro to help secure them, but that eventually peeled off. Surprisingly, the gaiters still stayed pretty well in place without it.

Altra Olympus 275, featuring how I’d attache my gaiters to the shoe laces.

All in all, I went through five pairs of shoes during my thru-hike. I probably could have squeezed the entire trail into four pairs, but I wanted my final 120 miles to be as comfortable and pain-free as possible. My general rule of thumb became replacing my shoes around every 500 miles. If I tried to push them much further, I’d quickly pay for it with blisters and foot fatigue.

After 2,200 miles, I was pretty happy with that system. Your shoes are one piece of gear I’d absolutely budget for before starting a thru-hike. They’re not going to last forever, and waiting until your feet are telling you it’s time for a new pair isn’t always the best strategy!

That covers the gear that carried me through the miles, but what about everything I wore along the way? From socks and underwear to the layers that got me through everything from hot Virginia afternoons to chilly New Hampshire nights, I’ll be breaking down my clothing system in the next post.

#8434. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8431. The 15 Best Spots to Hunt During the Peak of the Whitetail Rut

Published Oct 31, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The big-racked, muscled-up brute crashes through cover. Operating like a pedigreed cutting horse, he carves out two rival bucks and sends them packing for distant hills. Quickly, he returns to the small patch of cover where the wide-eyed estrus doe waits. The pair will likely stay in that obscure piece of real estate for the next 24 to 48 hours. That’s well away from most other deer — and hunters, who are focusing on better-looking ground with better traditional habitat hundreds of yards away. But it doesn’t have to be that way.

While traditional rut stands work just fine during the peak rut, other unorthodox spots can, too. Hunters should be aware of both sides of that coin. The rut-hunting playbook isn’t as small as some might believe. That’s why I’ve ranked the best 15 spots for peak-rut deer hunting.

Funnels and pinch-points are among the most orthodox stand locations during the rut. These are simply natural terrain features that encourage deer to travel through confined spaces. Of course, these are crucial for bowhunters, but they serve as excellent stand locations for gun hunters, too.

Because they’re so effective, however, funnels and pinch-points draw attention from a lot of hunters. On public land and shared private properties, such spots can become pressured and overhunted. In these scenarios, study a parcel’s pressure levels to determine if these spots are worth your time.

Does usually use the same, or the same few, bedding areas throughout the year. Over time, bucks learn where these locations are. During the rut, they’ll visit these in search of estrus does. Hunters should know where these are located, too.

Hunting doe bedding can be tricky, though. As with hunting any bedding area, you must get in early — long before daylight. Settle in on the downwind side of bedding areas and intercept bucks cruising these edges as they scent check for does. If multiple bedding areas are connected by cover, set up along these routes as bucks travel from one to the next.

Topography plays a major role in deer movement. Specific features can influence how, when, where, and why deer traverse certain routes. One such feature is an upper-third bench. This is a bench that, as it sounds like, spans the higher part of a ridge — but not the top of the ridge itself. Because morning thermals rise, this is a common area to catch bucks cruising the first few hours of the day. They can smell potential does down below. Furthermore, bucks often prefer the leeward side of the ridge because they can smell from both directions.

Similarly, lower-third benches are important, too. These are more effective hunting locations later in the day. In the evening, and sometimes even earlier in the afternoon, thermals fall. As the evening air pulls downward, scent collects and pools in the lowest points of the landscape. That’s why bucks travel along lower-level benches to detect potential does that are traveling, or have recently traveled, along the ridge above.

Now, back to those leeward ridges I mentioned above. These are simply the downwind sides of ridges, and they’re excellent locations to intercept deer travel patterns. These serve as great bedding areas as well as travel routes for deer, which mean they’re especially great stand locations during peak rut. Whether deer are bedding there, or merely using these as travel routes, hunters can intercept them.

Another hill-country feature to hunt is the famous saddle, or a low spot between two ridges. It might be where the same continuous ridge dips down and rises back up. Or it might be where two ridges running in different directions taper and meet. Either way, a saddle allows deer to pass through from one side or the other without having to climb up and over. It’s a smart spot to lie in wait for when they do.

Throughout the whitetail range, early successional habitat is vital to deer. Overgrown fields can provide that necessary edge cover. Oftentimes, these fill up with briars, brambles, grasses, and even forbs. Such growth might not look like much to us, but it provides good bedding cover and food sources. During the rut, bucks might even push estrus does into such areas to get them away from rival bucks.

Deer drink water year-round, but bucks get especially thirsty during the rut. All the cruising and chasing develops a need to rehydrate, and they frequent watering holes. Isolated water holes are especially attractive. Deer have limited options for finding water, particularly in dry conditions, and that increases the odds of shooting deer over one. You can hunt natural water sources or create your own, although creating these in huntable locations can require some serious strategy.

Deer spend most of their lives within cover, and that’s the best place to find a big deer. But during the rut, don’t overlook the power of a quality field-based food source. Standing soybeans, freshly cut corn, or any other crop with waist grain on the ground can be great. So can food plots, especially those planted with timely species. Hunting deer over food sources that are directly adjacent to quality bedding cover can produce sightings of a lot of deer, including mature bucks that are checking does or replenishing their energy.

Buck bedding areas are incredibly productive spots throughout the early season, pre-rut, and late season. Don’t overlook these areas during the rut. Often really old bucks will continue bedding in the same areas they have been using all fall, and only search for does at night. If they don’t find a hot doe, they retreat to the bedding areas they feel safest in.

So, continue to monitor the edges of these areas with trail cameras, and move in to hunt as necessary if you think a buck is still bedding there. Keep in mind that bucks and does often bed within the same block, but bucks tend to bed at higher elevations or in areas that are more advantageous.

I know, scrapes, go cold during the peak, rut, right? Sure, scraping activity drops off. But they don’t completely shut down. Bucks continue to check scrapes, and so do does. Does, and bucks that are between does, continue checking scrapes. So it doesn’t hurt to consider their prcense as a secondary or tertiary element when weighing strand locations, especially if scrapes are nearby an area you already plan to hunt.

Bucks don’t like competition. Because of this, older deer that know what they’re doing tend to push does into random areas the remainder of the deer herd rarely uses. Often this includes random brushy areas. Maybe it’s a fencerow, thick sinkhole, patch of grass, or other obscure — but maybe visually obvious — location.

Similarly, other small pockets of cover can be good, too. Even a half-acre, or even quarter-acre of cover can hold a breeding pair of deer. If it looks like a spot at least two deer could hide from other deer, and hunters, they might just be there. It might feel weird or unproductive to hunt these spots, but if you have good reason to, it just might pay off. Perhaps you saw a buck run into such a spot, maybe you didn’t. But during gun seasons, you should at least glass these areas or consider doing a deer drive through  these small pockets.

Drainage ditches are always overlooked. After all, who wants to hunt a hole in the ground? But drainage ditches with the right characteristics can hold deer. At the very least, deer might travel across or through it. Ditch crossings can be good all season long, but during the rut, it’s not uncommon for bucks to push does into brushy areas within ditches.

This is another area you wouldn’t expect a deer, but one worth considering. Brush piles with enough cover can hold a couple deer, and breeding pairs often shack up in such spots. Finding ways to hunt these can be difficult, but don’t overlook potential activity in such areas.

#8430. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

#8427. Octopus on the Camino Trail

We both slept exceptionally well last night. With only a short 9-miles stretch to Melide ahead of us, we were no rush to hit the trail.

Our first order of business was finding a cafe for breakfast. When we arrived, the place was packed, but the crowd cleared out quickly. Before long, we had the place to ourselves. We sat back and watched through the window as hordes of walkers passed by on the street outside. We were more than happy to let them get ahead so we could enjoy a quiet, more peaceful hike.

After a wonderful breakfast of eggs, great bacon, and hot coffee, our tramily members Robert and Jill caught up with us. By 9:30 AM, we were all back on the trail together.

Shortly after starting, we spotted a large group of hikers boarding a tour bus. They were likely being shuttled to a spot further down the trail to collect another passport stamp before heading on to Santiago. While the popular trail moto is “Hike Your Own Hike” (HYOH), this felt more like bus your own hike (BYOH)!

It was a gorgeous morning featuring blue bird skies, warm sun, and a crisp, cool breeze. Leaving Palas de Rei, the Camino entered a beautiful patch of woods along an ancient road. As we emerged from the forest, rolling hills and towering mountains opened up in the distance. I certainly didn’t expect this much dramatic typography on this Camino.

Our next milestone was the tiny medieval hamlet of San Xulian where we stepped inside a charming chapel to collect our first stamp for the day.

Leaving the village, we stepped onto a deeply sunken path with 15-foot-high earthen banks on either side—the result of centuries of footsteps wearing down the soil. These ancient roads are easily some of my favorite sections of the entire trek.

The trail then guided us through a magnificent eucalyptus forest filled with massive, towering trees. As we exited the canopy, we ran right back into the weekend crowds. Having developed our solid “trail legs” over hundreds of miles, Knockerz and I were moving at a much faster pace than the casual walkers. Passing them proved tricky, however, as large groups frequently blocked the narrow paths without realizing it.

As we approached Melide, we noticed numerous tour buses parked along the road. Apparently, this was where the “BYOH” crowd rejoined the path after skipping the 9 miles of walking in between! Melide is also a major trail milestone: it’s the official junction where the Camino Primitivo merges into the Camino Francés.

We arrived at 1:00 PM to a town bustling with energy. Knowing that siesta was fast approaching and the streets would soon turn into a ghost town, we set out to grab lunch immediately.

Knockerz was craving a hamburger, though she was disappointed to find the beef patty was blended with pork. Meanwhile, I couldn’t pass up Melide’s most famous specialty: Pulpo a la Gallega (Galician-style octopus). Traditionally boiled in large copper kettles, sliced into thick pieces, seasoned with paprika, and served on round wooden plates, it was delicious! Knockerz got a bit squeamish watching me eat the tentacles with their large suckers attached, but it was a highlight for me.

After lunch, we searched for Melide’s famous local pastry—a traditional anise-flavored donut (melindres)—but siesta had already begun and the bakeries were locked up tight. Fortunately, we found a tiny grocery store that remained open and picked up a bottle of Crianza Rioja wine.

It turned out to be a perfect afternoon with warm sun and a cool, refreshing breeze. We spent the rest of the day relaxing on the top terrace of our albergue, sipping Rioja while soaking in sweeping views of the distant Galician hills.

#8425. Matt Robertson Just Won $1.25 Million In the Champions Tournament. It’s The Largest First Place Payout in Professional Bass Fishing History

Published Oct 31, 2026 6:48 PM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

With a final day tally of 20 pounds, 2 ounces, and a total 3 day weight of 56 pounds and an ounce, Matt Robertson won a first-place payout of $1.25 million in the Champions bass fishing tournament on Old Hickory Lake in Tennessee. This is the largest first-place payout in the sport’s history and it represents an interesting turn in pro bass fishing.

Before we dive into the rest of the results, here’s what you need to know about the tournament and how it all came together.

It’s been just over 8 years since the professional bass fishing world effectively split the best anglers in the world into two separate organizations, the Bassmaster Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. In that time, new names have risen to the top of the leaderboards, and the old guard has won their fair share of events as well.

But the question that seemed to circulate year after year was who really is the best angler in the world?

Since the two organizations don’t cross-compete well, the answer remained shrouded in speculation and uncertainty. Sure, Jacob Wheeler might be the best at catching the most fish under the MLF BPT format, but could he still sack up 5 giants for 4 consecutive days in an Elite Series format? Would the young gun, Trey McKinney, give Wheeler or Kevin VanDam a run for their money in an MLF-style event?

The bass fishing world figured we’d never know, that is, until February of this year when World Bass Enterprises introduced The Champions Tournament. CEO Brian Bird announced the tournament, and an eye-popping $3.25 million purse to go along with it. Bass fishing fans from around the world started to pay attention.

To qualify for The Champions Tournament, Bassmaster Elite Series anglers and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers fished their respective 2026 tours throughout the year. After each event, they were awarded Angler of the Year points. The Champions Tournament lineup consisted of the top 25 in AOY points from the Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. The additional spots were filled based off of a “win and you’re in” ruling that applies to anglers who won one of the major events, but didn’t make the points cut.

Two additional anglers were selected through a random draw that WBE put on for those who pre-ordered the Pay-per-view streaming service.  Due to naming rights, the anglers were split into teams. Elite anglers were assigned ‘Team Stars’ and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers were assigned ‘Team Stripes’. The two randomly drawn anglers are Eric Giessing (Stars) and Kyle Carr (Stripes).

At the end of the event, a trophy was awarded to the top performing team, also “settling” the debate of which organization has the better anglers. For the 2026 Champions Tournament, Team Stars (Elite Series) has won bragging rights for the year.

“There has always been friendly competition and banter between the anglers on each tour, but no way to actually settle the score on the water,” MLF Bass Pro Tour 2025 Angler of the Year Jacob Wheeler said in a statement. “The opportunity to crown a true world champion across the entire sport is something our anglers have wanted for a very long time.”

The Champions Tournament was held on Old Hickory Lake, launching out of Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The launch and respective FanFest was full of attractions like a petting zoo, kids fishing area, inflatable archery, cornhole tournament, boat demos, and more. They even had the legendary Bill Dance fire off a cannon during the shotgun launch on the first day of competition.

Unsurprisingly, forward-facing sonar was addressed for this event, and seemingly played into a 50/50 outcome. For the first two days of competition, anglers were able to select which day they’d fish with live sonar, and which day they’d go without it. Then for the top 15 anglers fishing the final day, they got to use live sonar for 3 hours of competition.

To add to the pomp and circumstance, as if $1.25 million wasn’t enough, the weights also reset for the top 15 anglers heading into the final day. Making it truly anyone’s ballgame coming into Saturday. Old Hickory Lake put on quite a show for the first two days of competition, with largemouth, spotted bass, and smallmouth all making their way to the scales. The smallmouth dominant bags carried the most weight due to the minimum keeper size being 18-inches, while largemouth and spotted bass only needed to be 14-inches to make the cut.

The final day featured the following anglers fighting for the first place prize.

Matt Robertson, Ron Nelson, Bob Downey, Fisher Anaya, Pake South, Jason Christie, Trey Mckinney, Takahiro Omori, Kyle Welcher, Cole Sands, Chris Johnston, Cody Meyer, Bryan Thrift, Michael Neal, and Wesley Strader.

And while they all certainly wanted the top prize, the second place through seventh place payouts weren’t anything to scoff at either. Here is a look at the top 7 anglers, their final day weights, and their payouts after the final weigh-in. 15th place made a cool $20,000 and the payouts increased in $5,000 increments up to 7th.

1st Place: Matt Robertson (20-02) — $1.25 Million

3rd Place: Wesley Strader (11-02) — $300,000

4th Place: Trey Mckinney (11-0) — $200,000

5th Place: Michael Neal (10-10) — $100,000

While we put the largest professional bass fishing payout ever in the rearview mirror, it’s worth considering what The Champions Tournament means for bass fishing fans everywhere. Personally, there’s a bit of a shock factor involved. The payouts for the Bassmaster Classic and MLF Redcrest combined don’t even sniff the purse that was just awarded during this three-day event. That’s truly awe inspiring.

But what it really has shown me is that the two major organizations need to do some soul searching. If World Bass Enterprises can come out of nowhere and pull this off, perhaps it’s time to look at how they were able to do it successfully. Would fans pay a yearly subscription to watch a Pay-per-view Elite or BPT event? If so, could that increase the purses for those events and help the professionals in our sport actually make a living? I don’t see why not.

I know change is difficult for outdoorsmen and women, it’s in our nature to hold on to traditions and the status quo, but this weekend has shown me that there is a way to actually grow the sport of competitive bass fishing in a meaningful way. Now we’ll see if either organization actually has the guts to give it a try and truly make their anglers’ lives better.

As a final thought, I was blown away by the live coverage and the fanbase that showed up in-person and online, especially with the seasonality of this event. The bass fishing world was hungry for The Champions Tournament, and World Bass Enterprises pulled it off in epic fashion. I’m already looking forward to the 2027 lineup.

#8423. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition plan includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#8419. Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to a Top Deer Expert

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:14 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jeff Sturgis has the unique experience of living through dozens of deer seasons all at once. As the founder of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, he works with clients around the country to improve their deer hunting and private land habitat.

But before ever stepping foot on a property, Sturgis does in-depth interviews with these hunters to understand what they’d like to improve and what problems they’ve been having. Through this process, trends start to emerge.

Sturgis calls these problems “huntisms.” But they could also be described as misconceptions, misunderstandings, or straight up bad information. Whatever you want to call them, there are certain things that hunters get wrong when it comes to hunting mature bucks and managing habitat for those mature bucks.

So in this episode of the Outdoor Life Podcast, Sturgis will reference his decades of experience working on private land habitat as well as his time spent hunting on public ground to outline the most common and detrimental deer hunting mistakes. Heed his advice for a better season next year.

This common mentality of having to pound the woods and hunt all the time has saved a lot of big deer over the decades, Sturgis says.

“In some cases I can see this being partially true,” Sturgis says. “Maybe if you’re hunting public land, you’ve got ten spots and you’ve got the time to hunt freely.”

But if you’re hunting small parcels where you can’t afford to spook deer, then it’s usually smarter to stay home when hunting conditions are poor in order to not burn out your stands.

“There’s something to be said for minimizing your hunting, taking care of other priorities in life and expecting a higher rate of potential success because you’ve not over-pressured your stand locations.”

“It’s not just your stand locations [that you don’t want to burn out, it’s also your family, your career, your friends — it extends to an entire way to look at things. When I go out in the woods I want there to be a reasonable expectation that I’m going to shoot a deer for this reason.”

Sturgis says that if you have a “rutcation” planned where you know you’re going to hunt for a solid seven to nine days in a row, then it’s critical to reduce your impact. Instead of charging into a core area regardless of conditions, hunt spots where your scent cone won’t spook deer (because it’s blowing over a lake or off a cliff). And when conditions aren’t ideal, hunt transition areas where you could catch a big buck walking by, but you won’t spook deer near bedding areas or primary food sources.

Sturgis works with many clients who have the financial resources to grow and maintain sprawling food plots on their properties. Many of these clients believe that growing the maximum amount of food on the property will translate to holding the most amount of mature bucks in the fall.

But that’s not how it plays out most of the time. Growing too much summertime food — like big clover or bean plots — will increase the number of does and fawns on the property. During the summer and early fall, mature bucks don’t like to live on crowded food sources and bedding areas, Sturgis says.

“When you add summer food to good cover, you get a lot of does and fawns,” Sturgis says. “And those does and fawns that are here today are here to stay.”

These deer take up space and resources. Mature bucks will live on the fringes of these high-density deer areas but not establish a core zone there.

“Yeah, some bucks will come through during the rut. But bucks, the older they get, they don’t want that commotion and stress of a bunch of does and fawns. That’s why they live somewhere else.”

Sturgis says it’s better to focus on a comprehensive management strategy with proper deer cover, screening cover, sanctuaries, water holes, fall food, and yes, maybe some summer food plots, than it is to simply plant clover plots throughout the entire property.

“If you want to raise the population, add summer food. If you want to lower the population, get rid of summer food,” Sturgis says. “When I go to a client and see 20 acres of beans on their 200-acre property and we drive around and see over 100 does and fawns and only a couple bucks, they have a severe problem. I’d rather have those does and fawns be somewhere else in the summertime and shift over to the property starting in September and October.”

Don’t read this as an attack on food plots. Sturgis has written countless articles on the benefits of food plots, he’s got an online food plot class, he’s authored a book on the subject, and Whitetail Habitat Solutions sells food plot seed. So yes, food plots can be a critical element in consistently harvesting mature bucks.

But that doesn’t mean you should always hunt over them.

“This year I shot four bucks in four states with my bow … and not one of them was shot on a food plot,” Sturgis says. “Then I go to clients and they’re spending 90 percent of their hunts on food plots — and I’m not saying I never hunt on food plots — but the point is that the vast majority of my bucks are shot not in food plots.”

Sturgis tries to convince his clients to hunt away from food plots. Focusing instead on waterholes or funnels in the woods that might lead to food. This helps hunters spook fewer deer and see target bucks during daylight hours.

“Food plots have the greatest level of potential reward and the greatest level of risk,” Sturgis says. “If you spook out those food plots, you’ve just destroyed your property.”

Even though Sturgis has access to prime whitetail properties in the Midwest, he also hunts public land in Pennsylvania every year. In 22 seasons of hunting the same public area, Sturgis has shot 18 bucks.

It’s pretty common for him to bump into other hunters on these hunts, but he doesn’t sweat it. He just moves somewhere else. The key is being flexible and using tactics that match the conditions. For example, if it’s snowy and windy, Sturgis might still hunt through an area. If the woods are blanketed in crunchy leaves, he’ll opt to sit for the day.

One way that Sturgis makes sure that he avoids other hunters is by walking in at twilight (not in the dark).

“You don’t have to be to your spot before light,” Sturgis says. “When I’m walking into a spot like that, I don’t know what tree I’m going to be sitting under or in… So we’re walking into an area in daylight and still hunting [our way in].”

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season

It’s also important to remember that other hunters will bump deer long distances, not just a few hundred yards.

“Public land deer will get pushed a long way,” Sturgis says. “Especially in open woods. Where we hunt we can get 200-yard shots in the woods in some places. So when people push deer out there, they’re moving three quarters of a mile. So don’t think about just one little thicket. Think about how deer are moving in the big picture [across the landscape].”

#8418. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

#8413. I Shot the World Record Archery Elk While Hunting in Montana’s Belt Mountains

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:46 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Imagine yourself in a tree stand in Montana’s Belt Mountains. You know a bull elk is approaching because you’ve heard him bugle several times. The bugles were high-pitched one-tone squeals, indicating an immature bull. You’re after a trophy-class animal, but still you can’t help but get excited and you tighten the grip on your 73-pound compound bow.

A twig cracks behind you. You turn slowly and get the surprise of your life. There, not 30 yards away, stands a monstrous bull elk. His antlers are so massive that you wonder how he can hold up his head. This might be the next world-record elk!

You slowly twist the upper half of your body to your right. Trying hard to control your excitement, you try to draw your bow. You can’t! You’re in such an awkward position and your bow is so powerful that you can’t shoot!

That’s exactly the situation in which Dave Snyder, a Las Vegas fireman, found himself last year. But Snyder was no stranger to the frustrations involved in hunting trophy-size elk. He’d bowhunted the Belt Mountains seven previous times and each time he’d killed an elk. Two of those had been large enough to be listed in the Pope and Young Club record book of bow-killed big game. But this bull was larger than any other he’d seen.

Big-game hunting has been in Snyder’s blood ever since he was 12 years old, when he killed his first deer with an old .25/30 rifle in Nevada. Since he took up bowhunting 20 years ago, he has traveled all over the West in search of game. Among his trophies are an Alaskan moose and caribou, wild boars, bears, whitetail deer, Catalina goats and more mule deer bucks than some hunters see in a lifetime.

But elk hunting has been his first love ever since he killed his first bull, a five-pointer, in Colorado in 1972. From each hunt, he has drawn knowledge that has improved his skills. As he admitted to me last summer, his success at bowhunting elk has not been an accident.

For three years running, he bet friends as much as $500 that he’d kill, with his bow and arrow, a bull elk with at least five points on each antler. He won every time. Now he can’t find anybody to bet with him.

“It might seem pretentious for me to bet like that,” Snyder said, “but it’s really not. I’m just confident. If you know what you’re doing, a bowhunter has just as good a chance as a rifleman of taking a big bull—maybe even a better chance. Most gun hunters do well only if there’s a lot of snow. Bowhunters have the advantage of being able to hunt in September during the rut when elk are most vulnerable.”

Snyder’s Montana elk hunting success started almost by accident in 1974. He and another Las Vegas fireman, Mike Freeman, were having trouble with their truck’s carburetor, so they stopped by the side of the road and opened the hood. Dressed in full camouflage, they soon attracted the attention of a local logger, Dee Hills, who stopped to offer help. Hills had been very successful while rifle hunting for elk, but he was a novice bowhunter and had doubts about the killing power of arrows. Snyder and Freeman assured Hills that, yes, arrows kill elk very effectively.

“Why don’t you show me?” Hills suggested. “I know where the elk are and I’d be happy to take you there.”

After fixing the truck, the three hunters drove to Hills’ hunting area in the Belt Mountains. The next morning they hiked into a deep bowl and found a herd of elk almost immediately. But it wasn’t until afternoon that they got close to the animals. Soon a calf came ambling by Snyder and Hills.

“Aren’t you going to shoot?” Hills asked.

Soon the biggest cow in the herd walked to within 25 yards. Snyder drew his bow, aimed and released the arrow. It was a perfect hit and the animal dashed into the trees.

Snyder stifled a laugh. Hills didn’t understand that most arrow-shot animals streak away for 25 to 200 yards before piling up.

“No, that was a good hit,” Snyder said. “We’ll find her. But this will be a good chance for you to learn how to track.”

Snyder had to eat his words when they followed the cow. A wide trail of blood plainly led to where the elk lay dead only 75 yards from where she had been hit.

During the next few years, Snyder and some of his friends made a tradition of hunting together with Hills. They had remarkable success for bowhunters, something they attribute to careful observation and study.

One afternoon, Hills, Snyder and Larry Crim were fanned out on a ridge when a bull bugled. Snyder trotted directly toward the sound. Soon two bulls began bugling back and forth. Stalking carefully, Snyder soon got to within 40 yards of a small five-point but he guessed that the other bull was bigger by the sound of its voice. Suddenly the big bull bugled again within about 60 yards. Snyder sneaked closer but stopped when he saw several cows feeding. Knowing that herd bulls often circle their harems to keep intruders away, Snyder knelt and waited. Within seconds an exceptional six-point bull appeared, walking directly toward him. When the elk was about 25 yards away, he stopped and looked back toward his cows. Snyder quickly drew and released. The Satellite-tipped arrow smacked into the chest. The bull threw back his head and galloped through a barbwire fence before crashing to the ground. The bull’s antlers scored 357⅞ points with the standard measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club. The rack still ranks No. 17 in the club’s record book.

Most hunters probably would have taken a shot at the five-pointer, ruining their chances for the record-class bull. Snyder well understands the importance of passing up opportunities while trophy hunting. His other elk listed in the Pope and Young records was shot under similar circumstances.

Snyder was watching a big herd of cows when a five-point bull came within 20 yards, offering an easy broadside shot. The elk didn’t seem large enough to keep such a large harem to himself, so Snyder decided to pass up the shot. In seconds, a big six-point streaked around the cows, stopped within bow range and looked at the small bull. Then he looked toward Snyder, who was crouched in some undergrowth. When the elk turned again, Snyder shot. The arrow buried itself in the animal’s lungs. The bull covered less than 50 yards before dropping dead. Its antlers later scored 248⅞. A minimum score of 240 is required for listing in the record book.

Taking two record-book elk might satisfy many hunters but not Dave Snyder. He knew there were elk big enough to break the Pope and Young world record in Montana, a state that yields more truly exceptional bulls than any other. He felt his experience gave him just as good a chance as anybody else to find such an animal.

The Belt Mountains offer ideal habitat. Covered mostly by lodgepole pines, Snyder’s hunting area is broken up by dozens of logging clearcuts where elk find a good supply of the grass and low brush they need. Although the Belts aren’t as rugged and remote as some other elk-rich ranges in Montana, they offer plenty of cover in which crafty old bulls can hide from hunters and attain the old age necessary for growing outsize antlers.

The hunter had learned that elk are much more set in their habits than many sportsmen realize. In 1981, Snyder decided to take advantage of that by hunting from a tree stand near heavy elk sign.

On the first day of the season, Snyder carried a portable tree stand to a drainage about two miles from camp. He’d taken one of his record-book bulls there and had seen larger ones. Partway there, he walked to within 35 yards of an unusual spike bull with antlers at least two feet high. Snyder already had decided to shoot nothing smaller than a six-pointer for the first five days of the season but he was tempted to take the spike. After all, it would yield a freezer full of delicious meat and would make an unusual trophy. He finally decided to hold to his resolution and so watched the spike feed out of sight. But he had second thoughts about doing so.

Snyder set his stand in a tree overlooking a recently used elk wallow and several rubs—small trees had been debarked by elk preparing their antlers for the fighting and breeding season.

The next morning, Snyder rose before dawn, confident that he’d have action. But he couldn’t find the stand in the dark. By the time he finally found it, the sun was high and he decided to return to camp for lunch.

That afternoon, he and another Las Vegas bowhunter, Lynn Williams, decided to glass clearcuts and meadows. After half an hour or so, they saw an unusually large bull in a clearcut about 1½ miles away. The men decided to move closer to study the size of the antlers. By the time they reached the cut about an hour later, the bull was gone.

“I’m coming back here in the morning,” Williams said. “I know he’s a monster and, if he came here once, he’ll come again.”

The next morning Williams returned to the cut, Snyder to his tree stand, and Hills and Crim to a drainage that had yielded four elk in previous years, including Snyder’s biggest bull. The four hunters saw only one spike among them.

“I don’t think the rut has started,” Crim said during lunch. “We might as well hunt deer this afternoon. Elk hunting will be a lot easier after the rut starts anyway because the bulls will be bugling.”

Williams and Hills agreed, but Snyder couldn’t get the big bull out of his mind, so he decided to hunt elk while the others hunted deer. By 3:30 he was in the pines above the cut where he had seen the big elk. The elk sign was encouraging—fresh tracks and droppings and several newly destroyed saplings. Obviously elk had been feeding in the cut during the evenings. Normally, Snyder doesn’t like to hunt in or near feeding areas because the animals are extra-wary there, just as they are in bedding areas. Instead, he finds routes between feeding and bedding grounds and ambushes the animals as they pass. But daylight would soon run out, so he decided to find a good place to hide.

A game trail that led from the trees into the clearcut showed signs of heavy use. A spruce sapling, freshly mangled by a bull elk, stood next to the trail. Snyder happened to glance up. An old tree stand, made of two boards nailed between two trees, overlooked the trail. One board was hanging loose, nailed at only one end.

Snyder took a rope from his camouflage fanny pack, climbed the tree and tied the loose board tight. Gingerly, he put his whole weight on the stand to test it. In half an hour it would be too dark to shoot.

Less than 15 minutes later, he heard a faint bugle. It was more of a one-tone squeal than a bugle—typical of the sounds made by spike or raghorn bulls.

In reply, Snyder blew his own bugle, a simple tubular plastic whistle. The bull answered.

Snyder considered climbing to the ground where he’d have good mobility, but he knew he’d be harder to see 15 feet above the ground and that his scent would be more likely to drift high above the bull’s sensitive nose. The bull bugled again. Snyder bugled back and the elk immediately answered. Knowing that too much bugling can spook elk, he decided to wait for the bull to bugle on his own. A minute or so later, the elk squealed again, probably from within 200 yards.

Apprehensively, Snyder whistled for the third time. Again the bull answered with a high-pitched whistle. Snyder was certain the bull was a small one but he decided to prepare for a shot anyway. The bull bugled again, this time within 100 yards. Soon some limbs broke about 50 yards away and a faint sound of hooves on the ground could be heard. Snyder checked his bow and arrow one last time. The sound of his pulse in his ears made it difficult to hear the approaching bull. He fully expected the animal to offer an easy broadside shot on the trail to his left.

Suddenly, less than 30 yards away, a twig cracked behind him. Turning slowly, Snyder saw a magnificent bull with heavy mahogany antlers walk into the clearcut. Twisting to his right, Snyder started to draw his 73-pound Martin Cougar compound. Because of the awkward angle, he could draw it only partway.

The animal began walking slowly to the left. Snyder realized he’d have to twist back to his original position to shoot. He shifted his weight and the thing he had feared happened—the old tree stand creaked. The bull instantly stopped, swung around and stared right at him. Snyder didn’t dare to move. During that tense instant, another bull bugled no more than 200 yards away. The big elk turned and looked toward the sound and resumed walking to the left. Snyder prepared mentally to take a 25-yard broadside shot.

When the bull was behind some branches, it stopped and bugled the call of a spike elk.

“Come on, baby, just three more steps,” Snyder thought. “Just three more steps.”

The other bull bugled again. For no apparent reason, the heavy-antlered bull turned 180° and began walking back into the woods. This time Snyder drew his bow and then twisted around. He could see the bull between two trees that were perhaps 12 inches apart, so he crouched low to shoot under some branches, judged the distance at 45 yards, aimed and released. The orange aluminum arrow was visible during the first part of its flight but then disappeared. The bull hunched over as though he’d been hit and galloped across the clearcut, kicking up such a great cloud of dust that he was hardly visible as he fled. Moments after the bull disappeared into the trees, Snyder heard a crash. Had the magnificent animal fallen?

Snyder climbed to the ground and looked for blood and tracks. Already there was very little light and he could find no sign that he had hit the animal.

He returned to camp to get help and a Coleman lantern. Finding nobody there, he left a note and returned to his stand. He looked for his arrow or blood and found neither, so he searched a logging road that encircled the area but could find no sign that the animal had crossed it. Right then Crim, Williams and Hills arrived. The four men, carrying lanterns, spread out in a line and walked through the trees where Snyder had heard the crash. They knew they had to find the elk within a few hours or the massive animal’s body heat would ruin the game meat. They’d gone about 50 yards when Hills shouted, “There he is!”

The group walked up to the dead bull in silence. He’d fallen so hard that his antler tines had dug several feet under the sod. The antlers were so massive and his body so huge that the four hunters just stood there staring in awe. Finally Hills broke the silence: “Well, we better get to work or we’ll be here all night!”

To get the antlers out of the ground took the combined strength of all four men. The elk was so heavy that just dressing the carcass and dragging it 100 yards down a grassy slope took from 9 p.m. until 3 a.m.

The hunters decided to try winching the carcass off the ground so that the meat could cool. Fortunately, Williams had a powerful winch on the front of his four-wheel-drive pickup. They threw the winch cable over a branch in a large pine, attached the cable to the antlers and lifted the animal clear of the ground. Hanging this way, the bull looked as big as a full-grown rhinoceros.

Later, the bull yielded 560 pounds of boneless fat-free meat. Snyder estimates that the animal weighed well over 1,000 pounds, even after it had been field-dressed.

Read Next: The Real Story Behind the Casey Brooks Bull, the Pending World Record Elk

The 45-pound antlers were a bonus surprise. Though they had looked huge, none of the hunters had guessed that no bowhunter had ever killed a bigger bull. After a required 60-day drying period to allow for shrinkage, the rack was conservatively measured at 389⅞ points with the measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club.

That exceeded the score of the world-record elk taken by Jay Elmer of Arizona in 1980 (“Back-To-Back Bulls,” OUTDOOR LIFE, November 1981). The actual score verified by a panel of judges at the Pope and Young Club’s award banquet last spring was officially put at 391⅞. Snyder’s bull is now recognized as the world record. Even Dave Snyder should be satisfied with that.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.
