#8412. Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

“This is absolute madness,” said a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at New York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby showed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The New York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”

The first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

After making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

In March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The New York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby

Russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

The years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby

The distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

The arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

He lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:

I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

While Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

They later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”

In various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

“The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”

He has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa issues and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a new plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

Back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

The remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

He made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next issue. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

After 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The New York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he said. “It’s about to abruptly end.”

He is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

One big question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube

It might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

With just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

Then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Now that he has to confront a new question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”

#8410. Days 17–18: O Cebreiro, Fonfría, and a NERO

We could have eaten breakfast at the open café in La Faba as we walked past, but we decided to hold out for O Cebreiro. The steep climb up into town wasn’t as difficult as I remembered from 2017, but the village itself was clearly structured around tourist buses—and they appeared to have all left with their tourists. Cafés were shutting down, their tables piled with dirty dishes. “Go away!” one told us bluntly when we asked for a menu.

Trying every spot in sight, we finally landed back in the first one we had gone in, but now the kitchen was closed. We came back because it was the only open café that hadn’t locked its doors or shooed us out. Unfortunately, the power was off as an electrician was fiddling around in an open junction box. Our reward for the long morning climb was cold tuna empanada and cold bottled drinks—truly the saddest breakfast on the Camino. But we were happy for it, as the proprietor had also tried to send us away.

The beauty of the way into O Cebreiro was not matched by its hospitality

One bright spot was meeting Steve from Texas. I could tell by his distinct speech cadence that he was a practiced public speaker. It turned out he was a recently retired Church Administrator. Since I had served as both an executive pastor and senior pastor, we had plenty of shop to talk about. Steve had started way back in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, but after sustaining an injury, he was taking it slowly and relying on luggage forwarding to keep moving forward. He also spoke fluent Spanish and had intervened on our behalf when the lady was trying to tell us she couldn’t serve us because the power was out. “Isn’t there something cold they could have?”

The rest of the way, as they say, was downhill. We chose the older, traditional mountain path—the one I had walked back in 2017—rather than the newer route alongside the busy highway. It was serene and peaceful until it eventually rejoined the main road. Once we descended down O Cebreiro, The Way paralleled the pavement from a respectable half-mile distance, winding through quiet farm fields where the sound of traffic couldn’t reach us.

We reached Fonfría in late afternoon to stay at A Reboleira Hostel. Having arrived late, our private room was given away, but the hosts generously opened up an unused section of the dorm just for us, letting us pick our bunks. A few other pilgrims trickled in later making a total of 4 in a room built for 24, but it was so quiet we felt as though we had the entire place to ourselves.

Dinner was served in a traditional palloza—a round, thatched stone building identical to the ancient structures atop O Cebreiro. At least fifty pilgrims gathered on common tables. We sat with Charlie and Sarah, enjoying great conversation and getting to know them better, though sadly, our paths would diverge after that night.

The next day was a NERO—a “Near-Zero” rest day where we only had a short hour-and-a-half stroll on the trail, meaning there was no rush to get up and out early.

It was a wonderfully slow morning: breakfast, coffee, more toast, and more coffee. The Wi-Fi was fast and the café was warm, so why hurry? We rolled into O Biduedo by lunchtime and sat outside waiting for check-in at Casa Quiroga, watching the steady parade of pilgrims march past while I caught up on the sad state of world affairs via the New York Times on my phone.

Look carefully and you’ll see the cows coming home

As we sat there, local farmers herded cows down the narrow lane past us, only to return later, depositing fresh layers of manure across the pavement. In a way, it felt remarkably like reading the news, at least the manure part. I reminded myself of an old trail truth: It is good to bring the Camino home, but it is not good to invite home onto the Camino. Reading the news was precisely that—inviting the chaos of home into this sacred space. I hadn’t checked the headlines this whole trip, and I instantly regretted breaking the fast.

At Casa Quiroga, we checked into a lovely private room, ate, napped, and stepped out to explore the quiet hamlet. We spent the afternoon dodging fresh piles of cow manure and sneaking into an open, empty albergue to get our second stamp for the day. On the Camino, you are expected to collect two stamps daily in your credential, which can prove quite a logistical puzzle when resting in a tiny mountain village!

Back on pilgrim-watching duty outside, we met several friendly Australian couples who recounted stories of their cruises along the wild coast of Western Australia.

Later over dinner, Suzanne and I mapped out every relocation across our 40 years of married life. This Camino trek is our 40th-anniversary gift to each other, and with our house back home currently on the market as we contemplate another move, I wondered what wisdom we could extract from our past transitions.

We had never realized it until mapping it out on paper, but a clear pattern emerged: Suzanne was almost always the one who pulled us forward into a new chapter—leading us to Southwestern University, Ashesi University College in Ghana, back to Southwestern, and back to Ashesi again. Meanwhile, my role was recognizing when the Spirit was releasing us from a place or calling us to step down from an occupation. She provides the trajectory forward; I discern the moment to let go.

That’s a quiet blessing of the Camino, she longs to teach you things if you take the time to listen.

#8408. Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

No cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

So far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta

#8406. How to Beat the Worst Case of Buck Fever, According to This Archery Pro

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:29 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

When John Dudley was a kid, still learning how to hunt in Illinois, he had an encounter with a big buck that changed the trajectory of his bowhunting life. Dudley was hunting with a compound bow that was set too heavy—though he was able to draw the bow fine during practice.

When a stud buck casually walked into range, Dudley pulled with all of his might but he couldn’t get the bowstring back.

“He literally walks like 10 feet underneath my treestand … and I freakin’ pulled and tugged on that bow while my knees were clacking together,” Dudley says. “I had that thing pointed straight up in the air trying to pull it back. My heartbeat was hitting so hard I honestly thought I was going to need some stents or something by the time it was done.”

At first Dudley thought there was some sort of malfunction with his bow. As the buck walked off he examined the cams and the string. Then, with the deer (and the nerves) long gone, he simply grabbed the bow and drew it back without issue.

“You know when you have that nightmare that you can’t scream, well this was a living nightmare of John Dudley not being able to pull his bow back because he had buck fever that bad,” he says.

Fast forward a couple decades and Dudley is now an accomplished pro archer, a veteran whitetail hunter, and perhaps the most popular archery instructor in the country. Since that fateful Illinois bowhunt Dudley has learned a lot about shooting well under pressure during hunts and competitions. His hard-earned knowledge (which you can hear all about in the podcast episode below) will help you shoot your best when that big buck steps into your setup this fall.

When Dudley is sitting in his treestand he visualizes all the good scenarios that he hopes will happen. But this is far more than daydreaming about a giant buck turning broadside. Just like an athlete preparing for all the motions of a game, he visualizes each specific movement he’ll make under each possible scenario.

“I visualize myself getting a couple good ranges on him [as the buck comes in],” Dudley says. “I visualize making sure I grab my release the right way. I’m pivoting my feet the right way. And [the buck] is doing his thing as I’m able to slowly draw. And then I think about my shot process.”

With all the waiting we do in a treestand, there’s plenty of time to visualize and plan for a variety of shot scenarios.

“Sometimes I’m in a stand for two weeks before I have an opportunity and I’m constructing these things in my mind,” Dudley says. “You literally end up creating a vision. And when that happens, your conscious mind is already thinking about all the processes [you need to execute].”

In other words, when that giant buck finally does show, you won’t feel shocked, because you’ve already visualized it hundreds or thousands of times.

It’s almost a guarantee that every professional shooter in any shooting discipline has a shot process. As Dudley describes it, this is simply a series of words he says in his mind that coincide with actions he executes in order to make a perfect shot. Dudley’s shot process is this: 1) Stance; 2) Grip; 3) Shoulder; 4) Anchor; 5) Peep; 6) Pull and Finish.

Dudley learned the importance of having a process from Olympic medalist Lanny Bassham who wrote the book “With Winning in Mind” (which Dudley recommends for any shooter). The key is that saying the words and executing the movements is the work of the conscious mind. Activating the conscious mind helps prevent a shooter from “going on autopilot,” rushing the shot, punching the trigger, or simply blacking out.

You can and should adapt a shot process for your own needs. For example, OL gear editor and competitive archer Scott Einsmann’s process is: 1) Anchor; 2) Get it there (his cue to just get the aiming portion done with); 3) Feel alignment; 4) Okay, my shot can break anytime.

If you have a bad habit of getting excited and drawing back wildly, you might want to add a word like “smooth” to your shot process. If you have a tendency to get anxious about your pin floating around the target then you might want to add the word “float” to your process—reassuring yourself that it’s ok to let that pin float. The key is to have a shot process that works for you and to follow it on every single shot. Especially that shot on a giant buck.

Reciting a mantra is similarly useful. Just like running through a shot process, a mantra gives control to your conscious mind. You must choose to say your mantra.

For competitions, Dudley’s mantra is: “I shoot Xs because they make me feel good.”

When an animal comes in during a hunting scenario Dudley says the word “checkmate” to himself.

“When the animal presents that shot … I’m thinking ‘checkmate’, you know, game over,” he says. “Because that’s a positive affirmation that really reinforces your conscious thought process rather than sitting there thinking ‘Oh man this is the biggest buck I’ve ever seen.’”

But these tactics don’t eliminate the excitement and subsequent pressure you’ll likely feel when you see a shooter buck. The real key is training yourself to get comfortable while shooting under pressure.

“Think of buck fever like a hot bathtub,” Dudley says. “It might be scalding hot when you first put your toe into it. But if you just breathe and ease into it, eventually you’re going to acclimate and that water is going to feel OK.”

This is why Dudley recommends shooting in archery tournaments so you can “put yourself in a situation where you feel like you’ve been in the boiling pot before.”

If you have a high deer population where you hunt, or you just need to fill the freezer, shooting a few does with your bow is also a great way to get used to shooting under pressure. Your potential case of buck fever will likely be less extreme if you’ve cleanly killed a few does earlier in the season.

On the flipside don’t crank up the pressure on yourself during a hunt. In the treestand you want to feel positive, confident, and mellow.

“Don’t apply self-induced pressure,” Dudley says. “That’s the only pressure you really have control over. Most of the time buck fever or target anticipation is from pressure that you’re applying to yourself. It’s not like the animal is shooting [pressure] up at you. The best thing you can do is just positive self affirmation.”

In the days leading up to a big deer hunt Dudley makes sure to get in some practice sessions from a seated position and from an elevated position. This is because most whitetail shots will be from a ground blind or a treestand.

It’s important to know that shooting downhill or shooting from a seated position will induce more pin movement while you’re holding on target. But that’s OK if you’re used to it.

“It’s about mentally getting over that [pin movement],” Dudley says.

But there’s also value in practicing at long range even if you won’t be shooting at long range during a hunt. This is because flaws in your shooting will be more apparent at longer distances, and recognizing those flaws will help you correct them.

“I actually practice more at 80 than any distance I shoot at,” Dudley says.

Dudley believes in Chuck Adam’s theory that your effective range as a bowhunter is half the distance of your effective range in the backyard. In other words, if you’re able to shoot 8-inch groups at 80 yards in the backyard, you’ll be able to shoot 8-inch groups at 40 yards under a hunting scenario.

Plus, practicing at long range will boost your confidence when you move in for those realistic 20- and 30-yard shots. And really, at this point in the season, all practice is about building confidence for that moment of truth.

“Always practice at distances where you have confidence,” Dudley says. “Especially when you’re trying to instill confidence.”

#8400. ‘There Was No Controlling that Fish.’ Two Buddies Land One of the Largest Blue Marlin Ever Caught in Southern California

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:56 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

California fishing buddies Mike Mackenback and Matt Mackinga headed their 20-foot fishing boat into the Pacific at about daybreak on October 25. They were targeting wahoo, which had been hitting off the coast of southern California, but they were about to catch something much bigger.

“We ran south, looking for water temperature breaks where we believed wahoo would be found,” Mackenback tells Outdoor Life. “We were trolling by about 8 a.m., with three lines out – one a deep diving plug, a surface-skipping ‘Black Bart’ lure on another line, and a far back shotgun line with a lure.

“We were about 12 miles from San Pedro, trolling on a beautiful slick-ocean with clear water about 1,500-feet deep.”

Mackenback is a veteran marine boatman, having worked on tugboats and as a merchant marine. He knows boats and fishing and trolled fast at 8 knots for wahoo along a water temperature break from 73 to 75 degrees.

“The fish came up and smashed the surface skipping Black Bart lure about 30 minutes after we started,” says Mackenback, 29, who is now a real estate agent in Redondo Beach. “I thought at first it was a striped marlin until it jumped, then I knew it was huge – there was no controlling that fish as it ran 400 yards of line off a reel in one minute.”

Mackenback held the trolling rod which was set with a Shimano 30 Tiagra reel. It was spooled with 80-pound test Spectra braided line, with a top-shot of 50-pound test monofilament, and a 25-foot 200-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

Mackenback quickly realized they had hooked a huge blue marlin that was rapidly taking all the line off his reel, which was rigged for wahoo and much smaller striped marlin.

“I gave the rod to Matt, he went to the bow to fight the fish, and I turned the boat to chase after it,” Mackenback says. “The marlin was jumping and racing away, and I chased it with the boat for a few minutes while Matt tried to gain some of the line it took on those blistering runs.”

Matt kept the line tight on the marlin, and Mackenback got closer to the fish with his boat.

Then the marlin dove deep as it got a second wind during the fight.

“It almost spooled us twice,” says Mackenback. “Matt would gain line fighting the fish. I’d stay over it with the boat, and then it would dive deep again, and again, and again.

“We traded back and forth fighting the fish with the rod. We had no fighting belt or harness – just a small slide on the rod butt cushion. I didn’t think there was a 10 percent chance we’d catch and release it. My wahoo tackle wasn’t built for a giant blue marlin.”

One hour into the epic battle, the anglers decided to just follow the blue with their boat, trying to tire it out over time.

Almost two hours into the marlin battle they gained enough line on the fish that they could see its shiny blue color deep below in clear water. Then it dove deep again, and it was another 45 minutes before they spotted the fish near their boat.

“Suddenly the line went slack, and I thought it was gone,” Mackenback says. “We saw the swivel to the leader, grabbed it, and hauled on the leader to get it close.

“The fish was whipped, I knew it was gone as I was holding 600-pounds of blue marlin beside my 20-foot boat.”

They tried multiple times to revive the marlin for release. But the big blue fought until it was dead. There was no way they could get the marlin pulled up into their Grady-White boat. So, they lashed it to the side of their boat and ran slowly back to San Pedro’s Cabrillo Way Marina where they’d left that morning.

They notified the marina they were coming in with a huge marlin, and a crane was waiting for the anglers to haul the fish up and weigh it.

Their blue marlin measured more than 13 feet and weighed 595 pounds. It’s one of the largest blues ever caught off Southern California. Giant blues are believed to have moved into the region due to unusual water and weather conditions in this El Nino year.

In September 2015, a 648-pound blue marlin was caught 40 miles off San Diego by anglers aboard the boat Pegasus. A 692-pound blue was caught also during an El Nino year off the coast of Southern California.

Read Next: My Outboard Died — Just as We Hooked Up with a Giant Marlin

Mackenback and Mackinga cleaned and processed their marlin, and had some of it for dinner that night.

“We spent hours processing the marlin into steaks, and gave a lot of it to neighbors and friends,” says Mackenback. “We grilled marlin steaks that night and had a great cookout.”

#8395. New Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The new line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

This was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8394. Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:39 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’re five minutes into legal shooting with high hopes for your morning sit, then you hear it. A faint buzzing overhead. Eyes to the sky, you spot the drone hovering over your property. Suddenly, you’re less optimistic about your hunt.

[Insert neighbor] is up to no good again, you think. But is it actually who you think it is? How can you be sure? Basic, consumer-level drones can fly for miles. They can also spook deer and other wildlife on both public and private land.

Talk to landowners and deer hunters in Big Deer country and you’ll hear that drone usage has skyrocketed in recent years. Sure, there are a lot of folks flying drones legally during deer season. In many places it’s legal to fly a drone while attempting to recover a hit deer. Thermal drones are incredibly effective at this. But more and more, folks are using drones to scan other people’s properties in order to locate (and sometimes harass) big bucks.

Enter the drone defense system — a technology that defends against unwanted drones flying over a hunting property for all the wrong reasons.

Modern deer hunting and land management look vastly different than they did just a few years ago. Today, drones weave through several aspects of whitetail management and sometimes hunting and poaching, too. Drones are used for population surveys, property management, and deer recovery. These are common reasons deer hunters and land managers consult drone operators or fly their own drones. So long as laws are followed and ethical hunting is prioritized, there’s nothing wrong with any of that. In fact, when used properly, drones can be a net positive for whitetail herds, especially when sound management is the driving force.

But like with any new technology, some people are hellbent on using thermal drones for unethical purposes, namely, spying on the neighbor’s deer — and possibly even poaching them. That has sparked the need for the drone defense systems being promoted by Jack Huston, owner and operator of Midwest Deer Surveys.

“Most of the problem is people flying over property they don’t own or have permission to be on,” Huston says. “It’s not so much local landowners flying every day trying to know how to hunt a buck. It’s more people scouting the whole township, if you will.

“That’s a huge problem, and in my eyes, it’s trespassing,” Huston says. “People work so hard to have land to hunt. They work to make it ready for hunting season. Then, if somebody wants to just go fly a drone and buzz your deer, they can. And I don’t think that should be OK.”

The fast-growing popularity of drones in the hunting world creates a whole barrage of questions: What are the regulations around drones? Is it legal to fly over someone else’s property? Will wildlife agencies be using drone tracking tech to prevent poaching? Huston says the laws are very different from state to state.

“You know, Ohio is completely wide open — probably too much so,” Huston says. “Then there are some states that are what I call anti-drone.”

For example, Pennsylvania prohibits drone usage for any type of hunting, including tracking wounded deer.

Huston’s system allows a landowner to identify when a drone flies their property, and who the drone is registered to.

“I go all around the country doing deer surveys for landowners,” Huston said. “I talk to all of these people, and they are complaining about drones flying over their farms. A lot of times, these people are bigger landowners in the area, and people get curious.

“A lot of people pushed me to find a product that could essentially serve as a radar for drones. That is this product. People are setting them up at their house or barn and it just sits there and monitors the drone activity on that property, and all around it.”

The system picks up the transmission between the remote controller and the drone itself. It’s able to read that transmission and get the location of the pilot, location of the drone, the make of the drone, its serial number, and more. It records all of that and stores it for the user.

The collected drone detection information feeds back to an app on the landowner’s phone. It lets them know who’s flying, where they’re flying, and everything that’s going on in their airspace. It’s essentially a monitoring tool to alert landowners when someone is flying their property.

“With these drone detectors, we have real data of how many people are flying, and it’s certainly far more than I thought,” Huston says.

Huston says you can buy one of several drone defense system sizes and choose from options that cover roughly a 5-mile, 20-mile, or 40-mile radius.

“A lot of my customers are just geo-fencing their farm,” Huston says. “So, they’re creating a bit of a bubble around their property where they want to cover the skies.”

But as you can probably guess, setting up one of these systems isn’t cheap. Smaller stations start at about $5,000 while the bigger station will set you back about $12,000. Still, for a large property owner who has spent millions of dollars on owning the ground and implementing habitat work, the cost of a drone surveillance system is only a drop in the bucket.

While Huston doesn’t manufacture these himself (he works with a company on the manufacturing side), he helped establish and design the drone defense system.

Huston’s installations are already making positive impacts for some landowners who invest. He says there have been several instances where drones were detected, confirmations of illegal use were made, and law enforcement was called to intercept. Essentially, drones were being used to aid in poaching, and the drone defense systems assisted in prevention, and maybe eventual prosecution.

It does not take too much imagination to see how wildlife agencies and their game wardens might one day use similar drone detection systems to catch poachers and illegal fliers.

“Drones are the Wild West, right now,” Huston says. “I think, when the word gets out on these… It will push drones to be used how they’re supposed to be used.

Read Next: Drones Could Revolutionize How Hunters Recover Lost Deer … If They’re Not Banned First

“When I go out on my land, or my family’s land, I don’t want a drone bothering me,” Huston says. “And if there is one, I want to know who it is and solve that problem. This is the solution to that problem. Without it, people can get away with whatever they want.”

#8391. Iris Excursion

I close out 6 days of backpacking while diverting onto an alternate route to change things up.

Nature’s alarm system worked well through the night, perhaps too well. I felt pretty good that bears were unlikely to hang around a part of the forest so near to roads and homes. I’d been seeing deer consistently since I started hiking in New Jersey. I was awoken by leaf-crunching more times that I can remember. Each time I listened carefully to the steps, and each time I concluded that the animal was a deer. It was certainly too loud to be a squirrel, but not intrusive enough to be something as heavy as a bear. They took their sweet time moving on as well. At one point I was fed up to the point that I decided to unzip my tent and have a look. The sound of me unzipping my tent was enough for the animal to snort loudly – the hallmark sound of a deer warning other nearby deer of something out of the ordinary.

You might think spending 12 hours in my tent would be enough that I’d be off like a shot a first light. It sure would be nice to get back to my van early. Maybe I should have bought less cozy sleeping gear. Whatever the case, I made absolutely no haste this morning, quickly convincing myself to stay out of the 38 degree morning. I made breakfast, spilling a few ounces of water in my tent in the process which prompted a formidable snort of my own. I was glad that out of all the gear I’ve shed over the months, my large camping towel was not one of them.

It was almost 9:00AM when I got everything packed up and started making tracks on the AT. I was still on track to finish hiking in the 4:00 hour. However, there were some opportunities to save a bit of time on the way back. I decided it wasn’t worth taking the spur trail up to the High Point a second time, which opened up a shortcut back to the State Park HQ that was considerably flatter. I hardly felt the climb back up the ridge, the biggest issue was the thick layer of leaves spread across the trail.

Yesterday, as I neared the High Point State Park, I noticed several trails intersecting with the AT. One of them, the Iris Trail, crossed the AT several times. I studied the trail on FarOut and found that it was roughly the same distance, but definitely flatter. The hardest parts of the AT yesterday were exactly what the Iris Trail would be avoiding. I decided this would be a worthy alternate route that would give me some new things to see.

The first thing I noticed on this trail was how much easier it was than the AT. It was wider, graded nicely, and largely devoid of rocks. Unlike the AT, bikes are allowed, though I only saw one gentleman riding a bike on the trail. The trail passes Lake Rutherford, a surprisingly significant lake hidden up along the ridge. I was enjoying my easy ride on the Iris Trail until I felt my shoes sink into the trail. I didn’t react right away, taking another step, hoping the soft spot was a one-off. It was not. My shoe plunged several inches into wet mud. What looked like more pleasant, leafy trail was a streak of muddy trail several feet wide and about 20 feet long. I jumped off the trail, feeling my right foot suddenly overcome by cold water. I surveyed the trail, no sign of mud, except where I’d just stepped, the perfect trap. The mud had come up and over my toe box. I snorted again.

The creek that was discolored yesterday was back to normal clear flow today. Weird.

A pond near some pastures below the New Jersey High Point.

I made my way around the mud and continued on the Iris Trail, crossing the AT twice more before rejoining it for good at the Mashipacong Shelter. A few miles later I was taking in the view at the pavilion on Sunrise Mountain. Taking the Iris Trail allowed me to make up some time, I was now tracking toward getting back to the van at 3:30PM. Once I got back to the Culver Fire Tower, I knew it would all be downhill. I had managed to nurse my ankle along for the last two days, I just had to keep it that way as I made my way down the leafy rocks leading back to my van at Culvers Gap. I took my time and used Sunrise Mountain Road to save a few steps. I rewarded my early arrival with some basic hygiene activities – teeth brushing, and a shave with my electric razor. I still look a bit scraggly, I haven’t had a haircut since July, but that’s what hats are for.

It was a short drive to Newton, New Jersey for my usual serving of town food. I had picked this town because it also had a cafe open late – 10:00PM, where I proceeded to write up the blog posts from yesterday and today. I finished the day off by bagging up all my food for the upcoming week, one more Sunday chore off my back. Thanks to finding a good writing spot after each of my 3 2-day backpacking stints this week I would be able to have plenty of down time tomorrow.

The view west from near the Culver Fire Tower.

#8390. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#8388. Montana Man Banned From Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull

Published Nov 2, 2026 6:36 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A father and son who pleaded guilty to poaching in central Montana have lost their hunting privileges for a combined 24 years. Their poaching activity goes back years, but the investigation into the men started last year based on a tip from two bowhunters, who reported a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery season in September 2025.

“Lawful hunters are some of the most passionate outdoorsmen and women in existence. They’re very quick to report wildlife crimes and violations they see in the field,” Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks game warden and lead investigator Diego O’Brien tells Outdoor Life. “These two individuals, in my opinion, went above and beyond reporting the violation. They were very proactive with assistance in an area that I didn’t know very well. They proved to be incredible resources for me.”

Based on information provided by the two bowhunters, law enforcement located Billings resident Michael Letasky through a traffic stop. He matched the description of the man shooting the bull in the Little Belt Mountains, but he didn’t have the rack or any game meat. The bull was left to waste. (The two witnesses knew exactly where the dead animal was, but by then it was too late for wardens to salvage the meat.)

“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” O’Brien said in a statement. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation. They sacrificed their own hunting trip to ensure justice was served.”

The poached 6×6 bull met the state’s trophy standards. By state code, restitution for the illegal killing and possession or waste of trophy elk is $8,000. The only animal with a higher restitution than a 6×6 bull is a bighorn ram with at least three-fourths curl, which earns a penalty of $30,000.

In addition to the poached bull, Letasky also shot a raghorn with a firearm during the 2023 archery season, and he had an unreported black bear. During the investigation, wardens also found evidence against Letasky’s son, Kolton, of Austin, Texas.

Kolton Letasky killed a Montana buck in 2024 and a Montana bull in 2022 without the proper permits. He pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game and two counts of hunting without a license. His penalties include more than $3,000 in fines and no hunting for four years.

Read Next: YouTuber Poaching Bust Was a Case of ‘Wildlife Commercialization with a Modern Twist,’ Says Investigating Warden

The elder Letasky’s penalties are more severe. Michael Letasky plead guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game, two counts of hunting during a closed season and one count of wasting game. He owes more than $12,000 in fines and can’t hunt for 20 years.

#8386. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

#8384. Day 31: The Concert From the Castle

With the moon still plump and full, I set out through the mountains from the restful town I’d slept in.

It was daylight, and as I carefully descended the path strewn with loose rocks, I listened to the book that taught me about the Road to Santiago.

In the town before my destination, I planned to stop and eat breakfast. The cafe cats caught my attention as I approached. As the whole street came into view, I saw my Italian brother smiling at me. I ran to him and gave him a hug.

We always managed to stumble upon each other without planning, and I loved it.

When we made it to the city of Ponferrada, we went directly to the donativo albergue—San Nicolás de Flüe Pilgrims Hostel—to wait for it to open. The courtyard was large, with many trees, a large wooden totem, and a vine-covered sitting area. I went into the church nearby looking for a restroom. What I found, though, made me take a seat in the pew.

Within those tiny walls, an extraordinary mural was painted on the ceiling, depicting scenes from the Camino de Santiago, the four cardinal directions, the elements, and the stars. It stirred both the artist and the spiritual side within me.

When I went back to where we were relaxing, our Argentine brother had arrived. The three of us called ourselves “Familia Real”, the name emphasizing the bond we had created.

Once again, without planning, we were all together.

As a religious donativo albergue, I was placed on the woman’s side of the building. When I saw the name of the room I’d been assigned to, I couldn’t help but smile. “Cruz del Ferro.”

That place would forever hold a special place in my heart.

The brothers and I went on a side quest to a bodega overlooking the Castle of the Knights Templar.

After the siesta hours ended, I went to the Castle of the Knights Templar to embark on the tourist part of the day. I’d made it a few feet into the castle walkway when I saw my pilgrim friend below on the street. He was a musician who carried a flute with him everywhere, taking full advantage to play and sing and jam at every opportunity. I yelled down, asking him to play, but that was already his plan.

A man he met in the city joined him with a violin and I was entranced.

Standing on a castle wall, listening to music from artists I knew, with the city and mountains stretching out behind them, felt surreal.

That moment will forever be stamped into my memory.

After each song ended, I clapped from my perch on the castle wall, and the pilgrim smiled, skipping around with pride. His passion for music poured out of him with such a burning fire, and I felt lucky to witness it.

I knew I had a lot more to see, though, so I went on my way.

Exploring the exterior, I went level after level, corridor after corridor. I don’t like big houses, but now I want to live in a castle.

The secret passageways and rooms reminded me of the forts I used to build as a child.

And being on top of that tower overlooking the castle, the city, and the mountains?

I learned more about medieval culture than I ever had in my life. I explored an exhibit of a collection of books. The texts on display were all shapes and sizes, some as thick as my head, some smaller than a deck of cards.

Had it not been for exhaustion hitting me, I could’ve stayed for several more hours.

After 2.5 hours, though, I knew it was time to move on.

A grocery run on my way back to the albergue, a simple dinner in the chaotic kitchen, then quality time with my brothers.

The day had mirrored the life I’d grown accustomed to on the Camino.

In the kitchen at the end of the night, I met a fellow American for the first time. He’d seen me before in a different town and started the conversation with,

“You were working on your laptop and all I could think was ‘damn, she must be writing a book.’”

#8382. Secrets for Deer Hunting the Big Woods, According to a North Country Expert

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Hunting whitetails in the North Country forests of New England and the Upper Midwest is an undeniably challenging pursuit. Up there the landscapes are massive, think tens of thousands of acres of forest. Food sources and deer sign are more subtle. There are no edges of agricultural fields to target, and there might not even be stands of oaks dropping acorns. Lastly, deer densities are low, with some areas having maybe five deer per square mile.

It’s within this environment that Brett Joy, a member of the Just Hunt Club, has made a name for himself. Using a mix of old-school and modern hunting strategies, Joy has found success killing mature big woods bucks season after season.

I sat down with him for the most recent episode of the Outdoor Life podcast to learn his strategies for targeting mature bucks in the northwoods. Even if you don’t hunt big woods deer yourself, you can learn from Joy’s tactics and experience.

Joy uses digital maps to identify areas where two or three types of habitat converge.

“Whitetails, whether they’re in a cornfield in Iowa or on a mountain in New Hampshire, are edge habitat creatures,” Joy says. “They live on the edges, but those edges can look a lot different depending on where you are in the whitetails’ range.”

In the big woods, look for edges between hardwoods and softwoods, swamps and mature timber, mature timber and early successional growth (recently logged areas). Once you’ve identified these spots, scout them in person. Ideally, you’ll be a mile or more away from any road.

Joy believes that because the habitat is so vast in the big woods, bucks tend to have larger home ranges and core areas. They also have a variety of bedding areas — even in the early season. Whereas in the agricultural country, mature bucks tend to have only a couple woodlots and thickets where they like to bed.

“Our deer could bed on any different point of a mountain in any cut, in a swamp on any given day,” Joy says. “[Those bedding areas] could be miles apart day to day. They’re almost more of a nomadic deer … but they do have areas that they come back to year after year.”

The key is that even if you’re in a buck’s core zone, you might not see him for a week or more.

Like everywhere else in whitetail country, during the rut big woods bucks will travel between doe groups searching for does in estrus.

“But here, you may have only three does that live within 500 acres,” Joy says. So bucks have to cover more ground and do more checking. And this need to travel long distances makes rutting bucks more vulnerable.

“I like to hunt them during the rut and really focus on those areas they frequent when they’re traveling from A to B, or I hunt near one of those doe groups … and if you can find a big primary scrape or pinch point within the core area of those does, you can catch bucks going through there semi-consistently.”

Trail cameras are a critical component of Joy’s strategy because there’s essentially no visibility in the areas that he hunts. In other words, there are not places to glass from in the big woods.

“If I cared less about what buck I was targeting, I could hunt sign and not use cameras and be successful, but I really do rely on them heavily for my strategy,” he says.

Joy positions most of his cameras on large community scrapes because they serve as social gathering spots that will attract deer in vast landscapes. On top of that, Joy focuses on secluded, high-elevation areas that bucks tend to prefer.

Joy aims to run cameras from about October 15 through December 15, which gives him the full range of rut activity.

When you’re hunting the rut in the big woods, you need to have a good understanding of peak rut activity dates.

“What dictates everything is does coming into estrus,” Joy says. “And those bucks absolutely know those dates in this landscape and they will show up checking those doe groups on the same few days year after year.”

Joy conducted an in-depth trail camera survey using several years worth of his trail camera photos, plus his buddy’s photos to identify peak deer activity during the rut. He found that peak activity in his area was November 19th.

He then paired his trail cam data data with a biologist’s data on fawn conception dates in New Hampshire and he found that the peak conception date was November 19 as well.

“If I had to pick five or seven days, I’d put November 19th right in the middle of it,” Joy says.

Joy adds that he hasn’t witnessed a shutdown in activity due to lockdown. Bucks are covering the most ground during daylight during peak breeding dates.

But peak activity is different throughout whitetail country. You must examine your own trail camera photos and examine historical data to nail down the key dates where you hunt.

Read Next: North Woods Legend Hal Blood on Snow Tracking Bucks

“Now to kill deer in these landscapes you can’t just expect to hunt one weekend,” Joy says. You need probably a week of hunting and you need to hunt for the entire week, dark to dark, he says.

Joy will set up different stands within an area for different wind directions, but once he picks an area he sticks with it and does not jump around from spot to spot — even if he’s not seeing deer right away.

“Sometimes I don’t make a decision about where I’m going to sit until the day before … I’ll wait until I have all the information on a particular spot, but once I decide to [hunt there], that’s it. There’s no deviating. Once you start to doubt and jump around, you’re done,” Joy says. “The day you’re not there is the day he’ll come by.”

If you have good trail camera data and historical data on a spot, it makes it easier to commit to it for a week of hunting. Other keys to staying in the hunt long-term are: efficient access to your stand, good clothing to keep you warm, quality food to eat throughout the week, plenty of rest at night, and staying hydrated. Most importantly, you’ve got to keep the faith.

“Sitting in the cold for 11 or 12 hours a day, day after day, it really does wear on you and you start to doubt yourself and doubt your spot. You start to become negative, and once that stuff compounds … you’re not going to be there when that buck comes by.”

If you are able to stay patient and stick it out, there’s a good chance that an old northwoods buck will eventually walk by. And no matter how big his rack is, he’ll be a true trophy whitetail.

#8379. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.
